arXiv:2407.08338v1 [math.NT] 11 Jul 2024

Bounds in a popular multidimensional nonlinear Roth theorem

Sarah Peluse Address: Department of Mathematics
University of Michigan Email address: speluse@umich.edu , Sean Prendiville Address: School of Mathematical Sciences
Lancaster University Email address: s.prendiville@lancaster.ac.uk and Xuancheng Shao Address: Department of Mathematics
University of Kentucky Email address: xuancheng.shao@uky.edu
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

A nonlinear version of Roth’s theorem states that dense sets of integers contain configurations of the form xx, x+dx+d, x+d2x+d^{2}. We obtain a multidimensional version of this result, which can be regarded as a first step towards effectivising those cases of the multidimensional polynomial Szemerédi theorem involving polynomials with distinct degrees. In addition, we prove an effective “popular” version of this result, showing that every dense set has some non-zero dd such that the number of configurations with difference parameter dd is almost optimal. Perhaps surprisingly, the quantitative dependence in this result is exponential, compared to the tower-type bounds encountered in the popular linear Roth theorem.

1. Introduction

A long-standing programme in additive combinatorics concerns obtaining effective versions of the multidimensional Szemerédi theorem [FK78] and the polynomial Szemerédi theorem [BL96], as well as their common generalisation (also found in [BL96]); see for instance [Gow98, Gow22]. In this paper, we take a first step towards effectivising those cases of the multidimensional polynomial Szemerédi theorem involving polynomials of distinct degrees.

Theorem 1.1 (Density bound).

If A⊂{1,2,…,N}×{1,2,…,N}A\subset\mathopen{}\left\{1,2,\dots,N\mathclose{}\right\}\times\mathopen{}\left\{1,2,\dots,N\mathclose{}\right\} does not contain a triple of the form

(1.1) (x,y),(x+d,y),(x,y+d2)withd≠0,(x,y),\ (x+d,y),\ (x,y+d^{2})\quad\text{with}\quad d\neq 0,

then

|A|=O(N2/(logN)c).|A|=O\mathopen{}\left({N^{2}}/{(\log N)^{c}}\mathclose{}\right).

Here c>0c>0 is an absolute constant11 1 We expect that c=2−300c=2^{-300} is permissible..

Simultaneous to our work, Kravitz, Kuca and Leng [KKL] have obtained a result of this type for configurations of the form (x,y)(x,y), (x+P⁡(d),y)(x+P(d),y), (x,y+P⁡(d))(x,y+P(d)), where P∈ℤ⁡[d]P\in\mathbb{Z}[d] has an integer root of multiplicity one. Together, these constitute the first effective cases of the multidimensional polynomial Szemerédi theorem involving both a genuinely multidimensional configuration and a genuinely nonlinear polynomial.

We derive our density bound on taking ε=δ3/2\varepsilon=\delta^{3}/2 in the following stronger result, which proves the existence of a “popular” difference (with effective bounds).

Theorem 1.2 (Popular difference in two dimensions).

Let A⊂{1,2,…,N}×{1,2,…,N}A\subset\mathopen{}\left\{1,2,\dots,N\mathclose{}\right\}\times\mathopen{}\left\{1,2,\dots,N\mathclose{}\right\} with |A|⩾δ​N2|A|\geqslant\delta N^{2} and let 0<ε⩽1/20<\varepsilon\leqslant 1/2. Either N⩽exp(ε−O⁡(1))N\leqslant\exp\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{-O(1)}\mathclose{}\right) or there exists d≠0d\neq 0 such that

#{(x,y)∈A:(x+d,y),(x,y+d2)∈A}⩾(δ3−ε)N2.\#\mathopen{}\left\{(x,y)\in A:(x+d,y),(x,y+d^{2})\in A\mathclose{}\right\}\geqslant\mathopen{}\left(\delta^{3}-\varepsilon\mathclose{}\right)N^{2}.

Theorem 1.2 is a consequence of our more general Theorem 7.1, which we also use (in §7) to derive the existence of a popular difference in the one-dimensional context:

Theorem 1.3 (Popular difference in one dimension).

Let A⊂{1,2,…,N}A\subset\mathopen{}\left\{1,2,\dots,N\mathclose{}\right\} with |A|⩾δ​N|A|\geqslant\delta N and let 0<ε⩽1/20<\varepsilon\leqslant 1/2. Either N⩽exp(ε−O⁡(1))N\leqslant\exp\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{-O(1)}\mathclose{}\right) or there exists d≠0d\neq 0 such that

#{x∈A:x+d,x+d2∈A}⩾(δ3−ε)N.\#\mathopen{}\left\{x\in A:x+d,x+d^{2}\in A\mathclose{}\right\}\geqslant\mathopen{}\left(\delta^{3}-\varepsilon\mathclose{}\right)N.

We remark that the above exponential bound N⩽exp(ε−O⁡(1))N\leqslant\exp\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{-O(1)}\mathclose{}\right) is in sharp contrast to the tower-type bound necessary for linear three-term progressions, see [FPZ22].

As a corollary to Theorem 1.3, we obtain a new proof that subsets of {1,2,…,N}\mathopen{}\left\{1,2,\dots,N\mathclose{}\right\} lacking the nonlinear Roth configuration have at most polylogarithmic density, which is the main result of [PP22]. As in [PP22], our argument crucially relies on the advances made in [PP19].

The main input to all of the above results is the following inverse theorem, which characterises those functions that count many configurations of the form (1.1). Importantly, the quantitative dependence in this inverse theorem is polynomial. (In our inverse theorem, it turns out to be more natural to work with the asymmetric grid22 2 [N]:={1,2,…,N}[N]:=\mathopen{}\left\{1,2,\dots,N\mathclose{}\right\}. [N]×[N2][N]\times[N^{2}], rather than [N]×[N][N]\times[N].)

Let f0,f1,f2:ℤ2→ℂf_{0},f_{1},f_{2}:\mathbb{Z}^{2}\to\mathbb{C} be 1-bounded functions with support in [N]×[N2][N]\times[N^{2}]. Suppose that

The analogous one-dimensional inverse theorem [PP19, PP22] has been used by Krause, Mirek and Tao [KMT22] in their breakthrough work on pointwise convergence of bilinear polynomial ergodic averages. Remark 1.5 (The obstructions in our inverse theorem are necessary).

By removing the absolute value in (1.3), at the cost of introducing signs, one can re-phrase our inverse theorem as saying that if the counting operator for our configuration is large, as in (1.2), then the function weighting the (x+d,y)(x+d,y) term correlates with a function of the form

(x,y)↦e⁡(α​x)​ϕ​(y),(x,y)\mapsto e(\alpha x)\phi(y),

where α\alpha is “major arc at scale NN” and ϕ:ℤ→ℂ\phi:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} is 1-bounded. Similarly, the function weighting the (x,y+d2)(x,y+d^{2}) term correlates with a function of the form

(x,y)↦ψ⁡(x)​e​(β​y),(x,y)\mapsto\psi(x)e(\beta y),

where β\beta is major arc at scale N2N^{2} and ψ:ℤ→ℂ\psi:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} is 1-bounded.

Notice that the above formulation does not posit any structure for the 1-bounded functions ϕ\phi and ψ\psi. There is no hope in being able to extract further structure regarding these functions: their arbitrariness is necessary. This is exhibited in the following example.

Let ϕ:[N2]→{±1}\phi:[N^{2}]\to\mathopen{}\left\{\pm 1\mathclose{}\right\} be a random function that takes the value 1 with probability 1/2, independently as the argument ranges over [N2][N^{2}]. For (x,y)∈[N]×[N2](x,y)\in[N]\times[N^{2}] set

f0(x,y):=ϕ(x)ϕ(y)(−1)x+y,f1(x,y):=(−1)xϕ(y)andf2(x,y):=ϕ(x)(−1)y.f_{0}(x,y):=\phi(x)\phi(y)(-1)^{x+y},\quad f_{1}(x,y):=(-1)^{x}\phi(y)\quad\text{and}\quad f_{2}(x,y):=\phi(x)(-1)^{y}.

Then

∑x,y,df0​(x,y)​f1​(x+d,y)​f2​(x,y+d2)=∑x,y,d1[N]​(x)​1[N2]​(y)​1[N]​(x+d)​1[N2]​(y+d2)≫N4.\sum_{x,y,d}f_{0}(x,y)f_{1}(x+d,y)f_{2}(x,y+d^{2})=\sum_{x,y,d}1_{[N]}(x)1_{[N^{2}]}(y)1_{[N]}(x+d)1_{[N^{2}]}(y+d^{2})\gg N^{4}.

Yet for any “reasonable” notion of structured function ψ\psi, the randomness of ϕ\phi means that the fibre maps y↦f1​(x,y)y\mapsto f_{1}(x,y) and x↦f2​(x,y)x\mapsto f_{2}(x,y) almost surely do not correlate with ψ\psi.

1.1. Previous work

1.1.1. Density bounds for higher-dimensional configurations

Let us first put our density bound (Theorem 1.1) in context.

Given any two-point polynomial configuration (without congruence obstructions), it is likely that one can show that subsets of [N]n[N]^{n} lacking this configuration have at most polylogarithmic density. One way to prove this is to generalise Sárközy’s argument [Sár78] for the configuration x,x+d2x,x+d^{2}; see Lyall and Magyar’s [LM09] treatment of x¯,x¯+(d,d2,…,dn)\underline{x},\underline{x}+(d,d^{2},\dots,d^{n}) for an instance of this approach. It is also plausible that even stronger bounds could be obtained by adapting the argument of Bloom and Maynard [BM22], who have proved the current best known bounds in Sárközy’s theorem.

Longer linear configurations in ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} can be encoded as matrix progressions

x¯,x¯+T1​d¯,…​x¯+Ts​d¯,\underline{x},\ \underline{x}+T_{1}\underline{d},\ \dots\ \underline{x}+T_{s}\underline{d},

where TiT_{i} are n×nn\times n matrices with integer entries. As was demonstrated in [Pre15], provided that the TiT_{i} and their differences Ti−TjT_{i}-T_{j} (i≠ji\neq j) are all non-singular, one can extract density bounds for sets lacking these configurations by adapting the higher-order Fourier analysis techniques of Gowers [Gow01]. One may be able to synthesise this approach with that of [Pre17] in order to bound the density of sets lacking nonlinear matrix progressions of the form

x¯,x¯+T1​(d1k,…,dnk),…​x¯+Ts​(d1k,…,dnk),\underline{x},\ \underline{x}+T_{1}(d_{1}^{k},\dots,d_{n}^{k}),\ \dots\ \underline{x}+T_{s}(d_{1}^{k},\dots,d_{n}^{k}),

again provided that the TiT_{i} and their differences Ti−TjT_{i}-T_{j} (i≠ji\neq j) are all non-singular.

It is much harder to obtain quantitative bounds for sets lacking singular matrix progressions. Preceding this article and that of Kravitz-Kuca-Leng [KKL], there are only two results in this direction (for progressions of length greater than two). The first is due to Shkredov [Shk06] and obtains double-logarithmic bounds for sets lacking any three-point matrix progression, regardless of the singularity of the matrices and their differences. This very general result is deduced in [Pre15, Theorem B.2] from Shkredov’s much more concrete result which bounds the density of sets lacking two-dimensional corners:

(1.4) (x,y),(x+d,y),(x,y+d)withd≠0.(x,y),\ (x+d,y),\ (x,y+d)\quad\text{with}\quad d\neq 0.

Very recently, the first author [Pel24] obtained the first reasonable bounds for sets lacking a specific four-point singular matrix progression, namely L-shapes:

(1.5) (x,y),(x+d,y),(x,y+d),(x,y+2​d)withd≠0.(x,y),\ (x+d,y),\ (x,y+d),\ (x,y+2d)\quad\text{with}\quad d\neq 0.

Although this argument was carried out over the finite field model 𝔽pn×𝔽pn\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}, those conversant with the appropriate machinery will see that adapting the argument to the integer setting is now within reach, albeit technically demanding.

We believe the arguments of this paper open up the possibility of obtaining bounds for sets lacking polynomial progressions of the form

(1.6) x¯,x¯+P1​(d)​v¯1,…,x¯+Ps​(d)​v¯swithd≠0,\underline{x},\ \underline{x}+P_{1}(d)\underline{v}_{1},\ \dots\ ,\ \underline{x}+P_{s}(d)\underline{v}_{s}\quad\text{with}\quad d\neq 0,

where v¯1,…,v¯s\underline{v}_{1},\dots,\underline{v}_{s} are fixed integer vectors and the polynomials PiP_{i} have integer coefficients, zero constant term and (importantly) distinct degrees. Our configuration (1.1) corresponds to taking P1=dP_{1}=d, P2=d2P_{2}=d^{2}, v¯1=(1,0)\underline{v}_{1}=(1,0) and v¯2=(0,1)\underline{v}_{2}=(0,1). For the analogous problem over the finite field 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}, our paper corresponds to work of Han-Lacey-Yang [HLY21], and we posit that it is possible to obtain the analogue of Kuca’s more general result [Kuc24] in the integers. In this paper we make heavy use of the one-dimensional machinery developed in [PP19] for x,x+d,x+d2x,x+d,x+d^{2}, and for (1.6) we expect that the appropriate one-dimensional machinery is available in [Pel20].

1.1.2. Existence of a popular difference

We now turn to the context surrounding our popular difference results (Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.3). To our knowledge, the first results in this direction concern three-term and four-term arithmetic progressions [BHK05]. These results were obtained via ergodic methods and as a result concern the weaker notion of upper Banach density, rather than the lower density we deal with in Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.3. There have since been a number of ergodic works dealing with other configurations, see for instance [Fra08, Chu11, DLMS21]. In particular, Chu, Frantzikinakis and Host [CFH11] have proved the ergodic (and hence qualitative) analogue of Theorem 1.2.

Green [Gre05b] pioneered the use of arithmetic regularity to study these problems, proving the existence of a popular difference for three-term arithmetic progressions and thereby strengthening [BHK05] from upper Banach density to lower density. Green’s theorem states that for any ε>0\varepsilon>0 and any A⊂[N]A\subset[N] with |A|⩾δ​N|A|\geqslant\delta N, either N⩽C⁡(ε)N\leqslant C(\varepsilon) or there exists d≠0d\neq 0 such that

(1.7) #{x∈A:x+d,x+2d∈A}⩾(δ3−ε)N.\#\mathopen{}\left\{x\in A:x+d,\ x+2d\in A\mathclose{}\right\}\geqslant(\delta^{3}-\varepsilon)N.

Green and Tao [GT10] used higher-order Fourier analysis to obtain the analogous result for four-term arithmetic progressions. The result is false for longer progressions; see Ruzsa’s appendix to [BHK05].

In Green’s argument for (1.7), the constant C⁡(ε)C(\varepsilon) is bounded in terms of a tower of twos of height ε−O⁡(1)\varepsilon^{-O(1)}. This tower height was reduced to O⁡(log⁡(1/ε))O(\log(1/\varepsilon)) by Fox, Pham and Zhao [FP21, FP19, FPZ22], who went on to demonstrate (remarkably) that this bound is best possible.

In higher dimensions, existence of a popular common difference for certain non-singular matrix progressions of length 3 and 4 was established in [BSST22]. For corners (1.4), the ergodic version of a popular difference was studied by Chu [Chu11], with combinatorial analogues obtained by Mandache [Man21]. Both of these authors establish that the naive conjecture is not correct for the popular difference version of the corners theorem. The “correct” conjecture was emphatically addressed in [FSS+20]. In [SSZ21], linear configurations were classified according to when the naive conjecture is correct.

All of the above results concerning popular differences have either been qualitative or the bounds obtained have been tower-type. The only result we are aware of with reasonable bounds is due to Lyall and Magyar [LM13], and concerns two-point polynomial progressions in one dimension. Lyall and Magyar show that if PP is a polynomial with integer coefficients and zero constant term, then for any ε>0\varepsilon>0 and A⊂[N]A\subset[N] with |A|⩾δ​N|A|\geqslant\delta N, either there exists d∈ℤ∖{0}d\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\mathopen{}\left\{0\mathclose{}\right\} such that

#{x∈A:x+P(d)∈A}⩾(δ2−ε)N,\#\mathopen{}\left\{x\in A:x+P(d)\in A\mathclose{}\right\}\geqslant(\delta^{2}-\varepsilon)N,

or N⩽expexp(O(ε−1log(ε−1))N\leqslant\exp\exp\mathopen{}\left(O\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{-1}\log(\varepsilon^{-1}\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\right). We believe that by suitably adapting the methods of this paper, one should be able to replace this double exponential bound with N⩽exp(ε−O⁡(1))N\leqslant\exp\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{-O(1)}\mathclose{}\right). Determining the correct bound on NN seems an interesting problem, even in the simplest situation of xx, x+d2x+d^{2}. In forthcoming work by the second author, the third author and Mengdi Wang, we generalize Lyall and Magyar’s result to certain multi-point polynomial progressions, proving that if P1,⋯,PmP_{1},\cdots,P_{m} are polynomials with integer coefficients and zero constant terms with distinct degrees, then for any ε>0\varepsilon>0 and A⊂[N]A\subset[N] with |A|⩾δ​N|A|\geqslant\delta N, either there exists d∈ℤ∖{0}d\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\mathopen{}\left\{0\mathclose{}\right\} such that

#{x∈A:x+P1(d),⋯,x+Pm(d)∈A}⩾(δm+1−ε)N,\#\mathopen{}\left\{x\in A:x+P_{1}(d),\cdots,x+P_{m}(d)\in A\mathclose{}\right\}\geqslant(\delta^{m+1}-\varepsilon)N,

or N⩽expexp(O(ε−1))N\leqslant\exp\exp\mathopen{}\left(O\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{-1}\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\right).

2. An outline of our argument

All statements in this section are of a heuristic and informal nature, in particular much of what we write is, strictly speaking, false. To avoid obfuscating our sketch by tracking ranges of summation, we simply write 𝔼x​f​(x)\mathbb{E}_{x}f(x) to indicate a normalised sum, with the range of summation to be inferred from the context.

Given a set A⊂[N]2A\subset[N]^{2} of density δ:=|A|/N2\delta:=|A|/N^{2}, our starting point is to study the count

(2.1) 𝔼x,y,d​1A​(x,y)​1A​(x+d,y)​1A​(x,y+d2).\mathbb{E}_{x,y,d}1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x+d,y)1_{A}(x,y+d^{2}).

Traditionally in additive combinatorics, one compares this with the count of configurations lying in a random set of density δ\delta, which (after normalisation) is of order δ3\delta^{3}. If these counts are close, then one has a profusion of configurations in the set AA. If not, then we hope to show that AA has some exploitable structure. In a density increment argument, we typically exploit this by passing to a substructure where the density is larger. Iterating this argument eventually yields a substructure where the count of configurations is close to the random count, finishing our proof.

For many multidimensional configurations, we contend that the random count δ3\delta^{3} is not a useful comparison to make. One reason for this is that there are very unstructured sets that do not have the random number of configurations: taking an example from [Gre05a, §5], consider a product of random sets B1×B2B_{1}\times B_{2} where each Bi⊂[N]B_{i}\subset[N] has density δ\sqrt{\delta}. In the corners problem (1.4), one is forced to deal with these very loosely structured objects - they only possess the structure of a Cartesian product. However, the inverse theorem for our configuration (Theorem 1.4) says that the sets we need to deal with have more structure: they take the form B×PB\times P where P⊂[N]P\subset[N] is a dense arithmetic progression (i.e., of length proportional to NN and with small common difference) and B⊂[N]B\subset[N] is arbitrary. After moving to a grid with slightly larger step size, this purported “bad” set can be thought of as taking the form B′×[N′]B^{\prime}\times[N^{\prime}], where B′B^{\prime} has no exploitable structure.

With the above discussion in mind, and following [HLY21, Kuc24], we contend that it is more sensible to compare (2.1) with the following count, where we have essentially replaced the third indicator function 1A​(x,y+d2)1_{A}(x,y+d^{2}) with its average 𝔼y′​1A​(x,y′)\mathbb{E}_{y^{\prime}}1_{A}(x,y^{\prime}) on vertical fibres:

(2.2) 𝔼x,y,d​1A​(x,y)​1A​(x+d,y)​𝔼d′​1A​(x,y+d′+d2)≈𝔼x,y,d,d′​1A​(x,y)​1A​(x+d,y)​1A​(x,y+d′)≈𝔼x,y,x′,y′​1A​(x,y)​1A​(x′,y)​1A​(x,y′).\mathbb{E}_{x,y,d}1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x+d,y)\mathbb{E}_{d^{\prime}}1_{A}(x,y+d^{\prime}+d^{2})\\ \approx\mathbb{E}_{x,y,d,d^{\prime}}1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x+d,y)1_{A}(x,y+d^{\prime})\\ \approx\mathbb{E}_{x,y,x^{\prime},y^{\prime}}1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x^{\prime},y)1_{A}(x,y^{\prime}).

A (non-obvious55 5 See https://mathoverflow.net/questions/189222.) application of Hölder’s inequality gives that

𝔼x,y,x′,y′1A(x,y)1A(x′,y)1A(x,y′)⩾(𝔼x,y1A(x,y))3.\mathbb{E}_{x,y,x^{\prime},y^{\prime}}1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x^{\prime},y)1_{A}(x,y^{\prime})\geqslant\mathopen{}\left(\mathbb{E}_{x,y}1_{A}(x,y)\mathclose{}\right)^{3}.

Hence, we have a profusion of configurations, and, in particular, the existence of a popular difference, if (2.1) is ε\varepsilon-close to (2.2).

If (2.1) is not ε\varepsilon-close to (2.2), then, on setting

(2.3) f2​(x,y):=1A​(x,y)−𝔼d′​1A​(x,y+d′),f_{2}(x,y):=1_{A}(x,y)-\mathbb{E}_{d^{\prime}}1_{A}(x,y+d^{\prime}),

we have

|𝔼x,y,d1A(x,y)1A(x+d,y)f2(x,y+d2)|⩾ε.\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{x,y,d}1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x+d,y)f_{2}(x,y+d^{2})\mathclose{}\right|\geqslant\varepsilon.

At this point, we apply our inverse theorem (Theorem 1.4) to deduce the existence of α≈a/q\alpha\approx a/q with q⩽ε−O⁡(1)q\leqslant\varepsilon^{-O(1)} such that

𝔼x|𝔼yf2(x,y)e(αy)|⩾εO⁡(1).\mathbb{E}_{x}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{y}f_{2}(x,y)e(\alpha y)\mathclose{}\right|\geqslant\varepsilon^{O(1)}.

The function y↦e⁡(α​y)y\mapsto e(\alpha y) is approximately invariant under small shifts of the form y↦y+q2​d′y\mapsto y+q^{2}d^{\prime}, so by a little averaging, there exists N′⩾εO⁡(1)​NN^{\prime}\geqslant\varepsilon^{O(1)}N such that

(2.4) 𝔼x,y|𝔼|d′|<N′f2(x,y+q2d′)|⩾εO⁡(1).\mathbb{E}_{x,y}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{|d^{\prime}|<N^{\prime}}f_{2}(x,y+q^{2}d^{\prime})\mathclose{}\right|\geqslant\varepsilon^{O(1)}.

Equation (2.4) is saying that we can convolve f2f_{2} in the second coordinate with a long arithmetic progression of small common difference, in order to yield a function with large L1L^{1}-norm. Recall from (2.3) that f2f_{2} is, essentially, 1A1_{A} minus the convolution of 1A1_{A} in the second coordinate with the interval (−N,N)(-N,N). We can, therefore, use (2.4), together with approximate orthogonality properties of convolution, in order to obtain an energy increment:

𝔼x,y|𝔼|d′|<N′1A(x,y+q2d′)|2⩾𝔼x,y|𝔼|d|<N1A(x,y+d)|2+εO⁡(1).\mathbb{E}_{x,y}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{|d^{\prime}|<N^{\prime}}1_{A}(x,y+q^{2}d^{\prime})\mathclose{}\right|^{2}\geqslant\mathbb{E}_{x,y}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{|d|<N}1_{A}(x,y+d)\mathclose{}\right|^{2}+\varepsilon^{O(1)}.

We now repeat the above argument, this time focusing on the restricted counting operator

𝔼x,y​𝔼|d|<N′​1A​(x,y)​1A​(x+q​d,y)​1A​(x,y+q2​d2),\mathbb{E}_{x,y}\mathbb{E}_{|d|<N^{\prime}}1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x+qd,y)1_{A}(x,y+q^{2}d^{2}),

which counts configurations where the difference parameter is divisible by qq and ranges over a shorter interval. We compare this restricted counting operator with the restricted analogue of (2.2), namely

𝔼x,y​𝔼|d|,|d′|<N′​1A​(x,y)​1A​(x+q​d,y)​1A​(x,y+q2​d′).\mathbb{E}_{x,y}\mathbb{E}_{|d|,|d^{\prime}|<N^{\prime}}1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x+qd,y)1_{A}(x,y+q^{2}d^{\prime}).

Again, this comparison either yields a profusion of configurations in our set AA, or alternatively we have an energy increment of the form

𝔼x,y​|𝔼|d~|<N~​1A​(x,y+q2​q~2​d~)|2⩾𝔼x,y​|𝔼|d′|<N′​1A​(x,y+q2​d′)|2+εO⁡(1),\mathbb{E}_{x,y}\Bigl|\mathbb{E}_{|\tilde{d}|<\tilde{N}}1_{A}(x,y+q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2}\tilde{d})\Bigr|^{2}\geqslant\mathbb{E}_{x,y}\Bigl|\mathbb{E}_{|d^{\prime}|<N^{\prime}}1_{A}(x,y+q^{2}d^{\prime})\Bigr|^{2}+\varepsilon^{O(1)},

Iterating the energy increment nn times, we obtain a convolution whose energy is at least n​εO⁡(1)n\varepsilon^{O(1)}. Since the energy is bounded above by 1, the energy increment must terminate after at most n⩽ε−O⁡(1)n\leqslant\varepsilon^{-O(1)} steps. Setting q1:=qq_{1}:=q, q2:=q​q~q_{2}:=q\tilde{q} and so on, the iteration yields some common difference qnq_{n} of size

such that we have the comparison

|𝔼x,y𝔼|d|<Nn1A(x,y)1A(x+qnd,y)1A(x,y+qn2d2)−𝔼x,y​𝔼|d|,|d′|<Nn​1A​(x,y)​1A​(x+qn​d,y)​1A​(x,y+qn2​d′)|⩽ε.|\mathbb{E}_{x,y}\mathbb{E}_{|d|<N_{n}}1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x+q_{n}d,y)1_{A}(x,y+q_{n}^{2}d^{2})\\ -\mathbb{E}_{x,y}\mathbb{E}_{|d|,|d^{\prime}|<N_{n}}1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x+q_{n}d,y)1_{A}(x,y+q_{n}^{2}d^{\prime})|\leqslant\varepsilon.

This delivers a popular difference, since an argument using Hölder’s inequality again gives something of the form

𝔼x,y​𝔼|d|,|d′|<Nn​1A​(x,y)​1A​(x+qn​d,y)​1A​(x,y+qn2​d′)⪆δ3.\mathbb{E}_{x,y}\mathbb{E}_{|d|,|d^{\prime}|<N_{n}}1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x+q_{n}d,y)1_{A}(x,y+q_{n}^{2}d^{\prime})\gtrapprox\delta^{3}.

2.1. Paper organisation

Proving our inverse theorem (Theorem 1.4) occupies §§3-5. The first part of this argument (§3) shows that our configuration is controlled by a Gowers U5U^{5}-norm in the vertical direction. This uses the PET induction scheme of Bergelson-Leibman [BL96] together with the “quantitative concatenation” machinery developed in [PP19]. In §4, we use the degree lowering technique as developed in [PP19] to reduce the U5U^{5}-norm to a U1U^{1}-norm (after passing to a long progression with small common difference). In §5, we combine the results of the previous sections in order to derive our inverse theorem. Our energy increment argument is carried out in §6 and we deduce the existence of a popular common difference in §7. Notation that is used repeatedly is collected in Appendix A.

3. PET induction and U5U^{5}-control in the vertical direction

We begin by showing that our counting operator is controlled by a Gowers U5U^{5}-norm in the vertical direction. In order to establish the existence of a popular common difference (Theorem 1.2), it is convenient to work with a counting operator that incorporates a nicer weight than the sharp cut-off d∈[−N,N]d\in[-N,N] used in the inverse theorem stated in our introduction (Theorem 1.4).

As is exploited repeatedly in [PP19, PP22, Pel20], it is often more convenient to replace arbitrary bounded functions with dual functions, as these functions possess more structure. The next result shows that this is possible in Theorem 3.1. We eventually use this in §5.

Corollary 3.2 (Vertical U5U^{5}-control of the dual).

4. Degree lowering

The key result of this section is Lemma 4.5, which shows that we can replace the U5U^{5}-norm in Corollary 3.2 with the U1U^{1}-norm, after passing to a long subprogression of small common difference. Before proving this, we begin with a number of technical lemmas that underlie the argument.

Lemma 4.1 (Weyl bound).

Let μN\mu_{N} denote the probability measure

μN:=1N21[N]∗1−[N]=1N(1−|⋅|N)+.\mu_{N}:=\tfrac{1}{N^{2}}1_{[N]}*1_{-[N]}=\tfrac{1}{N}\mathopen{}\left(1-\tfrac{|\cdot|}{N}\mathclose{}\right)_{+}.

For any α,β∈𝕋\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{T} we have the implication

The following simple observation is used repeatedly in the remainder of the paper, and can be regarded as the key “reason” why Theorem 1.3 has exponential bounds, rather than the tower-type bounds encountered in the popular version of the linear Roth theorem [FPZ22]. It essentially allows us to show that we can pass from many “major arc” correlations to a single correlation: the major arcs line up. The reason underlying this is that the major arcs form a tiny fraction of all possible frequencies.

Lemma 4.3 (Pigeon-holing major arcs).

Let f1,…,fM:[−N,N]→ℂf_{1},\dots,f_{M}:[-N,N]\to\mathbb{C} be 1-bounded functions. For a fixed positive integer kk, let α,α1,…,αM∈𝕋\alpha,\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{M}\in\mathbb{T} be frequencies for which there are positive integers q1,…,qM⩽Qq_{1},\dots,q_{M}\leqslant Q such that ‖qm​(αm−α)‖𝕋⩽Q/Nk\mathopen{}\left\|q_{m}(\alpha_{m}-\alpha)\mathclose{}\right\|_{\mathbb{T}}\leqslant Q/N^{k} for each mm. 𝔼m∈[M]|𝔼|x|⩽Nfm(x)e(αmxk)|⩾1/Q.\mathbb{E}_{m\in[M]}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{|x|\leqslant N}f_{m}(x)e(\alpha_{m}x^{k})\mathclose{}\right|\geqslant 1/Q.

𝔼m∈[M]|𝔼|x|⩽Nfm(x)e(αm0xk)|≫1/QO⁡(1).\mathbb{E}_{m\in[M]}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{|x|\leqslant N}f_{m}(x)e(\alpha_{m_{0}}x^{k})\mathclose{}\right|\gg 1/Q^{O(1)}.

#{m∈[M]:αm=αm0}≫MQ−O⁡(1).\#\mathopen{}\left\{m\in[M]:\alpha_{m}=\alpha_{m_{0}}\mathclose{}\right\}\gg MQ^{-O(1)}.

By the popularity principle, there exists a set ℳ⊂[M]\mathcal{M}\subset[M] with |ℳ|⩾M2​Q|\mathcal{M}|\geqslant\frac{M}{2Q} such that for each m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M} we have

#{n∈𝒩m:ϕm(n)=ϕm}≫δO⁡(1)N.\#\mathopen{}\left\{n\in\mathcal{N}_{m}:\phi_{m}(n)=\phi_{m}\mathclose{}\right\}\gg\delta^{O(1)}N.

In particular

𝔼x∈[N]|∑dμN(d)fm(x+d)e(ϕmd2)|≫δO⁡(1).\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathopen{}\left|\sum_{d}\mu_{N}(d)f_{m}(x+d)e\mathopen{}\left(\phi_{m}d^{2}\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\right|\gg\delta^{O(1)}.

Applying Lemma 4.2, there exists q≪δ−O⁡(1)q\ll\delta^{-O(1)} such that ‖q​ϕm‖𝕋≪δ−O⁡(1)/N2\mathopen{}\left\|q\phi_{m}\mathclose{}\right\|_{\mathbb{T}}\ll\delta^{-O(1)}/N^{2}. Re-applying Lemma 4.3 gives some ϕ=ϕm0\phi=\phi_{m_{0}} such that

#{m∈ℳ:ϕm=ϕ}≫δO⁡(1)M\#\mathopen{}\left\{m\in\mathcal{M}:\phi_{m}=\phi\mathclose{}\right\}\gg\delta^{O(1)}M

Hence

#{(m,x)∈𝒩:ϕm(x)=ϕ}⩾∑m∈ℳ:ϕm=ϕ#{x∈𝒩m:ϕm(x)=ϕm}≫δO⁡(1)MN.\#\mathopen{}\left\{(m,x)\in\mathcal{N}:\phi_{m}(x)=\phi\mathclose{}\right\}\geqslant\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}:\phi_{m}=\phi}\#\mathopen{}\left\{x\in\mathcal{N}_{m}:\phi_{m}(x)=\phi_{m}\mathclose{}\right\}\gg\delta^{O(1)}MN.

∎

We are now in a position to prove our degree lowering lemma.

Lemma 4.5 (Degree lowering).

Let f0,f1:ℤ→ℂf_{0},f_{1}:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} be 1-bounded functions with

supp⁡(f0)⊂[N]×[N2]andsupp⁡(f1)⊂[−N,2​N]×[N2]\mathrm{supp}(f_{0})\subset[N]\times[N^{2}]\quad\text{and}\quad\mathrm{supp}(f_{1})\subset[-N,2N]\times[N^{2}]

Let μN\mu_{N} denote the probability measure

μN:=1N21[N]∗1−[N]=1N(1−|⋅|N)+.\mu_{N}:=\tfrac{1}{N^{2}}1_{[N]}*1_{-[N]}=\tfrac{1}{N}\mathopen{}\left(1-\tfrac{|\cdot|}{N}\mathclose{}\right)_{+}.

Define the dual function

Fx​(y)=F⁡(x,y):=∑dμN​(d)​f0​(x,y−d2)​f1​(x+d,y−d2),F_{x}(y)=F(x,y):=\sum_{d}\mu_{N}(d)f_{0}(x,y-d^{2})f_{1}(x+d,y-d^{2}),

a 1-bounded function supported on [N]×[2​N2][N]\times[2N^{2}]. Suppose that for some s⩾2s\geqslant 2 we have

𝔼x∈[N]​‖Fx‖Us​(ℤ)2s⩾δ​‖1[2​N2]‖Us​(ℤ)2s,\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathopen{}\left\|F_{x}\mathclose{}\right\|_{U^{s}(\mathbb{Z})}^{2^{s}}\geqslant\delta\mathopen{}\left\|1_{[2N^{2}]}\mathclose{}\right\|_{U^{s}(\mathbb{Z})}^{2^{s}},

where the UsU^{s}-norm is given by (A.5). Then, either N≪sδ−Os​(1)N\ll_{s}\delta^{-O_{s}(1)}, or there exists α∈𝕋\alpha\in\mathbb{T} and q≪sδ−Os​(1)q\ll_{s}\delta^{-O_{s}(1)} such that ‖qα‖𝕋≪sδ−Os​(1)/N2\mathopen{}\left\|q\alpha\mathclose{}\right\|_{\mathbb{T}}\ll_{s}\delta^{-O_{s}(1)}/N^{2} and

(4.8) 𝔼x∈[N]𝔼y∈[N2]|∑dμN(d)f1(x+d,y)e(αd2)|≫sδOs​(1).\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathbb{E}_{y\in[N^{2}]}\mathopen{}\left|\sum_{d}\mu_{N}(d)f_{1}(x+d,y)e\mathopen{}\left(\alpha d^{2}\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\right|\gg_{s}\delta^{O_{s}(1)}.
Proof.

Let us first assume that s⩾3s\geqslant 3. In this case, we claim that our assumptions imply that

(4.9) 𝔼x∈[N]‖Fx‖Us−1​(ℤ)2s−1≫sδOs​(1)‖1[2​N2]‖Us−1​(ℤ)2s−1.\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathopen{}\left\|F_{x}\mathclose{}\right\|_{U^{s-1}(\mathbb{Z})}^{2^{s-1}}\gg_{s}\delta^{O_{s}(1)}\mathopen{}\left\|1_{[2N^{2}]}\mathclose{}\right\|_{U^{s-1}(\mathbb{Z})}^{2^{s-1}}.

Given this claim, we intend to iterate in order to arrive at the case in which s=2s=2, so that

(4.10) 𝔼x∈[N]‖Fx‖U2​(ℤ)4≫sδOs​(1)‖1[2​N2]‖U2​(ℤ)4.\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathopen{}\left\|F_{x}\mathclose{}\right\|_{U^{2}(\mathbb{Z})}^{4}\gg_{s}\delta^{O_{s}(1)}\mathopen{}\left\|1_{[2N^{2}]}\mathclose{}\right\|_{U^{2}(\mathbb{Z})}^{4}.

Returning to the proof of (4.9), since we may assume that N≪s1N\ll_{s}1 does not hold, we have

‖1[2​N2]‖Us​(ℤ)2s≫sN2​s+2.\mathopen{}\left\|1_{[2N^{2}]}\mathclose{}\right\|_{U^{s}(\mathbb{Z})}^{2^{s}}\gg_{s}N^{2s+2}.

Expanding the definition of the UsU^{s}-norm (A.5), and using the fact that FxF_{x} is supported on [2​N2][2N^{2}], gives

𝔼|h1|<2​N2⋯𝔼|hs−2|<2​N2𝔼x∈[N]‖Δh1,…,hs−2Fx‖U24≫sδN6.\mathbb{E}_{|h_{1}|<2N^{2}}\dotsm\mathbb{E}_{|h_{s-2}|<2N^{2}}\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathopen{}\left\|\Delta_{h_{1},\dots,h_{s-2}}F_{x}\mathclose{}\right\|_{U^{2}}^{4}\gg_{s}\delta N^{6}.

Applying the U2U^{2}-inverse theorem [PP19, Lemma A.1], there exists

𝒩⊂((−2​N2,2​N2)s−2∩ℤs−2)×[N]\mathcal{N}\subset\left((-2N^{2},2N^{2})^{s-2}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{s-2}\right)\times[N]

of size |𝒩|≫sδN2​s−3|\mathcal{N}|\gg_{s}\delta N^{2s-3} and a function ϕ:ℤs−1→𝕋\phi:\mathbb{Z}^{s-1}\to\mathbb{T} such that for every (h¯,x)∈𝒩(\underline{h},x)\in\mathcal{N} we have

(4.11) |∑yΔh¯Fx(y)e(ϕ(h¯;x)y)|≫sδN2.\biggl|\sum_{y}\Delta_{\underline{h}}F_{x}(y)e\bigl(\phi(\underline{h};x)y\bigr)\biggr|\gg_{s}\delta N^{2}.

Set T:=⌈Cs​δ−1​N2⌉T:=\mathopen{}\left\lceil C_{s}\delta^{-1}N^{2}\mathclose{}\right\rceil, with CsC_{s} an absolute constant taken sufficiently large to ensure that, on rounding ϕ⁡(h¯,x)\phi(\underline{h};x) to the nearest fraction of the form t/Tt/T, the inequality (4.11) remains valid.

Summing over 𝒩\mathcal{N} and applying the dual-difference interchange inequality [PP19, Lemma 6.3], we deduce that

∑(h¯0,x),(h¯1,x)∈𝒩|∑y,dμN​(d)​Δ(0,h¯0−h¯1)​f0​(x,y−d2)Δ(0,h¯0−h¯1)f1(x+d,y−d2)e(ϕ(h¯0;h¯1;x)y)|≫sδOs​(1)N4​s−5,\sum_{(\underline{h}^{0},x),(\underline{h}^{1},x)\in\mathcal{N}}\biggl|\sum_{y,d}\mu_{N}(d)\Delta_{(0,\underline{h}^{0}-\underline{h}^{1})}f_{0}(x,y-d^{2})\\ \Delta_{(0,\underline{h}^{0}-\underline{h}^{1})}f_{1}(x+d,y-d^{2})e\bigl(\phi(\underline{h}^{0};\underline{h}^{1};x)y\bigr)\biggr|\gg_{s}\delta^{O_{s}(1)}N^{4s-5},

where

ϕ(h¯0;h¯1;x):=∑ω∈{0,1}s(−1)|ω|ϕ(h¯ω;x)andh¯ω:=(h1ω1,…,hsωs).\phi(\underline{h}^{0};\underline{h}^{1};x):=\sum_{\omega\in\mathopen{}\left\{0,1\mathclose{}\right\}^{s}}(-1)^{|\omega|}\phi(\underline{h}^{\omega};x)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\underline{h}^{\omega}:=(h_{1}^{\omega_{1}},\dots,h_{s}^{\omega_{s}}).

Changing variables from yy to y+d2y+d^{2} and taking maxima, there exist yy and h¯1\underline{h}^{1} such that

∑(h¯0,x)∈𝒩|∑dμN(d)Δ(0,h¯0−h¯1)f1(x+d,y)e(ϕ(h¯0;h¯1;x)d2)|≫sδOs​(1)N2​s−3.\sum_{(\underline{h}^{0},x)\in\mathcal{N}}\mathopen{}\left|\sum_{d}\mu_{N}(d)\Delta_{(0,\underline{h}^{0}-\underline{h}^{1})}f_{1}(x+d,y)e\bigl(\phi(\underline{h}^{0};\underline{h}^{1};x)d^{2}\bigr)\mathclose{}\right|\gg_{s}\delta^{O_{s}(1)}N^{2s-3}.

Thus, there exists 𝒩′⊂𝒩\mathcal{N}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{N} of size 𝒩′≫sδOs​(1)N2​s−3\mathcal{N}^{\prime}\gg_{s}\delta^{O_{s}(1)}N^{2s-3} such that for each (h¯0,x)∈𝒩′(\underline{h}^{0},x)\in\mathcal{N}^{\prime} we have

|∑dμN(d)Δ(0,h¯0−h¯1)f1(x+d,y)e(ϕ(h¯0;h¯1;x)d2)|≫sδOs​(1).\mathopen{}\left|\sum_{d}\mu_{N}(d)\Delta_{(0,\underline{h}^{0}-\underline{h}^{1})}f_{1}(x+d,y)e\bigl(\phi(\underline{h}^{0};\underline{h}^{1};x)d^{2}\bigr)\mathclose{}\right|\gg_{s}\delta^{O_{s}(1)}.

By Lemma 4.4, there exists 𝒩′′⊂𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime}\subset\mathcal{N}^{\prime} of size ≫sδOs​(1)N2​s−3\gg_{s}\delta^{O_{s}(1)}N^{2s-3} and ϕ∈𝕋\phi\in\mathbb{T} such that for any (h¯0,x)∈𝒩′′(\underline{h}^{0},x)\in\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime} we have ϕ⁡(h¯0,h¯1,x)=ϕ\phi(\underline{h}^{0};\underline{h}^{1};x)=\phi. In particular, when restricted to the set 𝒩′′\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime}, the function ϕ\phi satisfies

ϕ(h¯0;x)=ϕ−∑ω∈{0,1}s−2∖{0}(−1)|ω|ϕ(h¯ω;x).\phi(\underline{h}^{0};x)=\phi-\sum_{\omega\in\mathopen{}\left\{0,1\mathclose{}\right\}^{s-2}\setminus\mathopen{}\left\{0\mathclose{}\right\}}(-1)^{|\omega|}\phi(\underline{h}^{\omega};x).

For fixed xx, the right-hand side of this identity is low rank in h¯0\underline{h}^{0} according to the terminology preceding [PP19, Lemma 6.4].

Summing over h¯\underline{h} such that (h¯,x)∈𝒩′′(\underline{h},x)\in\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime} in (4.11), we deduce the existence of low-rank functions ψx:ℤs−2→𝕋\psi_{x}:\mathbb{Z}^{s-2}\to\mathbb{T} such that

(4.12) 𝔼x∈[N]𝔼|h1|<N2⋯𝔼|hs−2|<N2|∑yΔh¯Fx(y)e(ψx(h¯)y)|≫sδOs​(1)N2.\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathbb{E}_{|h_{1}|<N^{2}}\dotsm\mathbb{E}_{|h_{s-2}|<N^{2}}\mathopen{}\left|\sum_{y}\Delta_{\underline{h}}F_{x}(y)e\bigl(\psi_{x}(\underline{h})y\bigr)\mathclose{}\right|\gg_{s}\delta^{O_{s}(1)}N^{2}.

Employing the inequality stated in [PP19, Lemma 6.4] then gives

𝔼x∈[N]‖Fx‖Us−12s−1≫sδOs​(1)N2​s.\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathopen{}\left\|F_{x}\mathclose{}\right\|_{U^{s-1}}^{2^{s-1}}\gg_{s}\delta^{O_{s}(1)}N^{2s}.

This proves the claim (4.9).

By iterating (4.9), our initial assumption of large UsU^{s}-norm yields a large U2U^{2}-norm, as in (4.10). Moreover, we note that when running the argument with s=3s=3, the inequality (4.12) becomes

𝔼x∈[N]|𝔼|y|⩽2​N2Fx(y)e(ψxy)|≫sδOs​(1),\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{|y|\leqslant 2N^{2}}F_{x}(y)e\bigl(\psi_{x}y\bigr)\mathclose{}\right|\gg_{s}\delta^{O_{s}(1)},

where for each xx, our application of Lemma 4.4 gives some qx≪sδ−Os​(1)q_{x}\ll_{s}\delta^{-O_{s}(1)} with ‖qxψx‖𝕋≪sδ−Os​(1)/N2\mathopen{}\left\|q_{x}\psi_{x}\mathclose{}\right\|_{\mathbb{T}}\ll_{s}\delta^{-O_{s}(1)}/N^{2}. Once more applying Lemma 4.3, we may assume that ψx=ψ\psi_{x}=\psi is constant in xx, so that

𝔼x∈[N]|∑yFx(y)e(ψy)|≫sδOs​(1)N2.\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\biggl|\sum_{y}F_{x}(y)e\bigl(\psi y\bigr)\biggr|\gg_{s}\delta^{O_{s}(1)}N^{2}.

Expanding the dual function FxF_{x}, changing variables in yy and employing the triangle inequality to bring the sum over yy outside the absolute value, we derive (4.8). ∎

5. Inverse theorems for our counting operator

Degree lowering (Lemma 4.5) can be combined with vertical U5U^{5}-control of the dual function (Corollary 3.2), and a little Fourier analysis, in order to prove an inverse theorem for the function weighting the (x+d,y)(x+d,y) term in our counting operator.

Theorem 5.1 (Counting operator inverse theorem, I).

Let f0,f1,f2:ℤ2→ℂf_{0},f_{1},f_{2}:\mathbb{Z}^{2}\to\mathbb{C} be 1-bounded functions and let μN\mu_{N} denote the probability measure

μN:=1N21[N]∗1−[N]=1N(1−|⋅|N)+.\mu_{N}:=\tfrac{1}{N^{2}}1_{[N]}*1_{-[N]}=\tfrac{1}{N}\mathopen{}\left(1-\tfrac{|\cdot|}{N}\mathclose{}\right)_{+}.

Write

ΛN​(f0,f1,f2):=𝔼x∈[N]​𝔼y∈[N2]​∑dμN​(d)​f0​(x,y)​f1​(x+d,y)​f2​(x,y+d2).\Lambda_{N}(f_{0},f_{1},f_{2}):=\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathbb{E}_{y\in[N^{2}]}\sum_{d}\mu_{N}(d)f_{0}(x,y)f_{1}(x+d,y)f_{2}(x,y+d^{2}).

If |ΛN(f0,f1,f2)|⩾δ\mathopen{}\left|\Lambda_{N}(f_{0},f_{1},f_{2})\mathclose{}\right|\geqslant\delta, then either N≪δ−O⁡(1)N\ll\delta^{-O(1)} or there exists β∈𝕋\beta\in\mathbb{T} and q≪δ−O⁡(1)q\ll\delta^{-O(1)} such that ‖q​β‖𝕋≪δ−O⁡(1)/N\mathopen{}\left\|q\beta\mathclose{}\right\|_{\mathbb{T}}\ll\delta^{-O(1)}/N and

(5.1) 𝔼y∈[N2]|𝔼x∈[−N,2​N]f1(x,y)e(βx)|≫δO⁡(1).\mathbb{E}_{y\in[N^{2}]}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{x\in[-N,2N]}f_{1}(x,y)e\mathopen{}\left(\beta x\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\right|\gg\delta^{O(1)}.
Proof.

In order to avoid tracking the range of summation, we assume that

supp⁡(f0)⊂[N]×[N2]andsupp⁡(f1)⊂[−N,2​N]×[N2]\mathrm{supp}(f_{0})\subset[N]\times[N^{2}]\quad\text{and}\quad\mathrm{supp}(f_{1})\subset[-N,2N]\times[N^{2}]

Notice that this affects neither the hypothesis nor the conclusion of the theorem.

By vertical U5U^{5}-control of the dual function (Corollary 3.2), our assumptions give that

𝔼x∈[N]​‖Fx‖U5​(ℤ)25≫δO⁡(1)​‖1[2​N2]‖U5​(ℤ)25,\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathopen{}\left\|F_{x}\mathclose{}\right\|_{U^{5}(\mathbb{Z})}^{2^{5}}\gg\delta^{O(1)}\mathopen{}\left\|1_{[2N^{2}]}\mathclose{}\right\|_{U^{5}(\mathbb{Z})}^{2^{5}},

where

Fx​(y)=F⁡(x,y):=∑dμN​(d)​f0​(x,y−d2)​f1​(x+d,y−d2).F_{x}(y)=F(x,y):=\sum_{d}\mu_{N}(d)f_{0}(x,y-d^{2})f_{1}(x+d,y-d^{2}).

By degree lowering (Lemma 4.5), either N≪δ−O⁡(1)N\ll\delta^{-O(1)} or there exists α∈𝕋\alpha\in\mathbb{T} and q≪δ−O⁡(1)q\ll\delta^{-O(1)} with ‖q​α‖𝕋≪δ−O⁡(1)/N2\mathopen{}\left\|q\alpha\mathclose{}\right\|_{\mathbb{T}}\ll\delta^{-O(1)}/N^{2} such that

𝔼x∈[N]𝔼y∈[N2]|∑dμN(d)f1(x+d,y)e(αd2)|≫δO⁡(1).\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathbb{E}_{y\in[N^{2}]}\mathopen{}\left|\sum_{d}\mu_{N}(d)f_{1}(x+d,y)e(\alpha d^{2})\mathclose{}\right|\gg\delta^{O(1)}.

By the popularity principle and Lemma 4.2, for each y∈[N2]y\in[N^{2}] there exist qy≪δ−O⁡(1)q_{y}\ll\delta^{-O(1)} and βy∈𝕋\beta_{y}\in\mathbb{T} with ‖qy​βy‖𝕋≪δ−O⁡(1)/N\mathopen{}\left\|q_{y}\beta_{y}\mathclose{}\right\|_{\mathbb{T}}\ll\delta^{-O(1)}/N such that

𝔼y∈[N2]|𝔼x∈[−N,2​N]f1(x,y)e(βyx)|≫δO⁡(1).\mathbb{E}_{y\in[N^{2}]}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{x\in[-N,2N]}f_{1}(x,y)e(\beta_{y}x)\mathclose{}\right|\gg\delta^{O(1)}.

Pigeon-holing in the major arcs (Lemma 4.3), there exists β∈𝕋\beta\in\mathbb{T} and q≪δ−O⁡(1)q\ll\delta^{-O(1)} with ‖q​β‖𝕋≪δ−O⁡(1)/N\mathopen{}\left\|q\beta\mathclose{}\right\|_{\mathbb{T}}\ll\delta^{-O(1)}/N such that

𝔼y∈[N2]|𝔼x∈[−N,2​N]f1(x,y)e(βx)|≫δO⁡(1).\mathbb{E}_{y\in[N^{2}]}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{x\in[-N,2N]}f_{1}(x,y)e(\beta x)\mathclose{}\right|\gg\delta^{O(1)}.

The result follows. ∎

We now use the inverse theorem for the function weighting the (x+d,y)(x+d,y) term to obtain an inverse theorem for the function weighting the (x,y+d2)(x,y+d^{2}) term.

Theorem 5.2 (Counting operator inverse theorem, II).

Let f0,f1,f2:ℤ2→ℂf_{0},f_{1},f_{2}:\mathbb{Z}^{2}\to\mathbb{C} be 1-bounded functions and let μN\mu_{N} denote the probability measure

μN:=1N21[N]∗1−[N]=1N(1−|⋅|N)+.\mu_{N}:=\tfrac{1}{N^{2}}1_{[N]}*1_{-[N]}=\tfrac{1}{N}\mathopen{}\left(1-\tfrac{|\cdot|}{N}\mathclose{}\right)_{+}.

Write

ΛN​(f0,f1,f2):=𝔼x∈[N]​𝔼y∈[N2]​∑dμN​(d)​f0​(x,y)​f1​(x+d,y)​f2​(x,y+d2).\Lambda_{N}(f_{0},f_{1},f_{2}):=\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathbb{E}_{y\in[N^{2}]}\sum_{d}\mu_{N}(d)f_{0}(x,y)f_{1}(x+d,y)f_{2}(x,y+d^{2}).

If |ΛN(f0,f1,f2)|⩾δ\mathopen{}\left|\Lambda_{N}(f_{0},f_{1},f_{2})\mathclose{}\right|\geqslant\delta, then either N≪δ−O⁡(1)N\ll\delta^{-O(1)} or there exists α∈𝕋\alpha\in\mathbb{T} and q≪δ−O⁡(1)q\ll\delta^{-O(1)} such that ‖q​α‖𝕋≪δ−O⁡(1)/N2\mathopen{}\left\|q\alpha\mathclose{}\right\|_{\mathbb{T}}\ll\delta^{-O(1)}/N^{2} and

𝔼x∈[N]|𝔼y∈[2​N2]f2(x,y)e(αy)|≫δO⁡(1).\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{y\in[2N^{2}]}f_{2}(x,y)e\mathopen{}\left(\alpha y\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\right|\gg\delta^{O(1)}.
Proof.

We may assume that

supp⁡(f0)⊂[N]×[N2],supp⁡(f1)⊂[−N,2​N]×[N2],supp⁡(f2)⊂[N]×[2​N2].\mathrm{supp}(f_{0})\subset[N]\times[N^{2}],\quad\mathrm{supp}(f_{1})\subset[-N,2N]\times[N^{2}],\quad\mathrm{supp}(f_{2})\subset[N]\times[2N^{2}].

Define the dual function

G⁡(x,y):=∑dμN​(d)​f0​(x−d,y)​f2​(x−d,y+d2).G(x,y):=\sum_{d}\mu_{N}(d)f_{0}(x-d,y)f_{2}(x-d,y+d^{2}).

Then, by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality:

δ⩽|1N3∑x,yf1(x,y)G(x,y)|≪(1N3∑x,yG(x,y)G⁡(x,y)¯)1/2=ΛN(f¯0,G,f¯2)1/2.\delta\leqslant\mathopen{}\left|\frac{1}{N^{3}}\sum_{x,y}f_{1}(x,y)G(x,y)\mathclose{}\right|\ll\mathopen{}\left(\frac{1}{N^{3}}\sum_{x,y}G(x,y)\overline{G(x,y)}\mathclose{}\right)^{1/2}=\Lambda_{N}\mathopen{}\left(\overline{f}_{0},G,\overline{f}_{2}\mathclose{}\right)^{1/2}.

Hence, by our first inverse theorem (Theorem 5.1), either N≪δ−O⁡(1)N\ll\delta^{-O(1)} or there exists β∈𝕋\beta\in\mathbb{T} and q≪δ−O⁡(1)q\ll\delta^{-O(1)} such that ‖q​β‖𝕋≪δ−O⁡(1)/N\mathopen{}\left\|q\beta\mathclose{}\right\|_{\mathbb{T}}\ll\delta^{-O(1)}/N and

𝔼y∈[N2]|𝔼x∈[−N,2​N]G(x,y)e(βx)|≫δO⁡(1).\mathbb{E}_{y\in[N^{2}]}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{x\in[-N,2N]}G(x,y)e\mathopen{}\left(\beta x\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\right|\gg\delta^{O(1)}.

Expanding the dual function, changing variables and employing the triangle inequality, we have

𝔼x∈[N]𝔼y∈[N2]|∑dμN(d)f2(x,y+d2)e(βd)|≫δO⁡(1).\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathbb{E}_{y\in[N^{2}]}\mathopen{}\left|\sum_{d}\mu_{N}(d)f_{2}(x,y+d^{2})e(\beta d)\mathclose{}\right|\gg\delta^{O(1)}.

By the popularity principle and Lemma 4.2, for each x∈[N]x\in[N] there exist qx≪δ−O⁡(1)q_{x}\ll\delta^{-O(1)} and αx∈𝕋\alpha_{x}\in\mathbb{T} with ‖qx​αx‖𝕋≪δ−O⁡(1)/N2\mathopen{}\left\|q_{x}\alpha_{x}\mathclose{}\right\|_{\mathbb{T}}\ll\delta^{-O(1)}/N^{2} such that

𝔼x∈[N]|𝔼y∈[2​N2]f2(x,y)e(αxy)|≫δO⁡(1).\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{y\in[2N^{2}]}f_{2}(x,y)e(\alpha_{x}y)\mathclose{}\right|\gg\delta^{O(1)}.

Pigeon-holing in the major arcs (Lemma 4.3), there exists α∈𝕋\alpha\in\mathbb{T} and q≪δ−O⁡(1)q\ll\delta^{-O(1)} with ‖q​α‖𝕋≪δ−O⁡(1)/N2\mathopen{}\left\|q\alpha\mathclose{}\right\|_{\mathbb{T}}\ll\delta^{-O(1)}/N^{2} such that

𝔼x∈[N]|𝔼y∈[2​N2]f2(x,y)e(αy)|≫δO⁡(1).\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{y\in[2N^{2}]}f_{2}(x,y)e(\alpha y)\mathclose{}\right|\gg\delta^{O(1)}.

The result follows. ∎

The previous two inverse theorems concern the global count of configurations. As indicated in §2, our strategy for proving Theorem 1.2 is to focus on counting configurations where the difference parameter is divisible by a small positive integer qq and is localised to an interval shorter than NN. We therefore require an inverse theorem for this localised counting operator. We also take this opportunity to replace correlation with major arcs by convolution with a Fejér kernel, which facilitates the energy increment argument in Theorem 6.1. Making these adjustments to our inverse theorem is the purpose of the next result.

Theorem 5.3 (Large localised count gives a large convolution).

Let f0,f1,f2:ℤ2→ℂf_{0},f_{1},f_{2}:\mathbb{Z}^{2}\to\mathbb{C} be 1-bounded functions with support contained in [−N1,N1]×[−N2,N2][-N_{1},N_{1}]\times[-N_{2},N_{2}] where N1⩾N21/2N_{1}\geqslant N_{2}^{1/2}. Suppose that for some positive integers q,Mq,M with q​M⩽N21/2qM\leqslant N_{2}^{1/2} we have

|∑x,y,dμM(d)f0(x,y)f1(x+qd,y)f2(x,y+q2d2)|⩾δN1N2.\mathopen{}\left|\sum_{x,y,d}\mu_{M}(d)f_{0}(x,y)f_{1}(x+qd,y)f_{2}(x,y+q^{2}d^{2})\mathclose{}\right|\geqslant\delta N_{1}N_{2}.

Then there exists a positive integer q~\tilde{q} with q~≪δ−O⁡(1)\tilde{q}\ll\delta^{-O(1)} such that for any positive integer M~\widetilde{M}, either M~≫δO⁡(1)​M\widetilde{M}\gg\delta^{O(1)}M or

(5.2) ∑x,y|∑d~μM~2(d~)f2(x,y+q2q~2d~)|≫δO⁡(1)N1N2.\sum_{x,y}\mathopen{}\left|\sum_{\tilde{d}}\mu_{\widetilde{M}^{2}}(\tilde{d})f_{2}(x,y+q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2}\tilde{d})\mathclose{}\right|\gg\delta^{O(1)}N_{1}N_{2}.

Here μM\mu_{M} and μM~2\mu_{\widetilde{M}^{2}} denote the Fejér kernels defined in (A.7).

Proof.

By a change of variables, we may average our operator over additional shifts, to deduce that

|∑x,y𝔼x′∈[M]𝔼y′∈[M2]∑dμM(d)f0(x+qx′,y+q2y′)f1(x+q(x′+d),y+q2y′)f2​(x+q​x′,y+q2​(y′+d2))|⩾δ​N1​N2.\Bigl|\sum_{x,y}\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\in[M]}\mathbb{E}_{y^{\prime}\in[M^{2}]}\sum_{d}\mu_{M}(d)f_{0}(x+qx^{\prime},y+q^{2}y^{\prime})f_{1}(x+q(x^{\prime}+d),y+q^{2}y^{\prime})\\ f_{2}(x+qx^{\prime},y+q^{2}(y^{\prime}+d^{2}))\Bigr|\geqslant\delta N_{1}N_{2}.

Hence, on setting

fix,y,q​(x′,y′):=fi​(x+q​x′,y+q2​y′),f_{i}^{x,y,q}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}):=f_{i}(x+qx^{\prime},y+q^{2}y^{\prime}),

we have that

(5.3) |∑x,yΛM(f0x,y,q,f1x,y,q,f2x,y,q)|⩾δN1N2.\Bigl|\sum_{x,y}\Lambda_{M}\mathopen{}\left(f_{0}^{x,y,q},f_{1}^{x,y,q},f_{2}^{x,y,q}\mathclose{}\right)\Bigr|\geqslant\delta N_{1}N_{2}.

We note that, since q​M⩽N21/2⩽N1qM\leqslant N_{2}^{1/2}\leqslant N_{1} and each fif_{i} is supported on [−N1,N1]×[−N2,N2][-N_{1},N_{1}]\times[-N_{2},N_{2}], the set of pairs (x,y)∈ℤ2(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2} that contribute to (5.3) is contained in [−2​N1,2​N1]×[−2​N2,2​N2][-2N_{1},2N_{1}]\times[-2N_{2},2N_{2}]. Thus, by the popularity principle, there exists a set 𝒫⊂[−2​N1,2​N1]×[−2​N2,2​N2]\mathcal{P}\subset[-2N_{1},2N_{1}]\times[-2N_{2},2N_{2}] of size ≫δ​N1​N2\gg\delta N_{1}N_{2} such that

|ΛM(f0x,y,q,f1x,y,q,f2x,y,q)|≫δfor all (x,y)∈𝒫.\mathopen{}\left|\Lambda_{M}\mathopen{}\left(f_{0}^{x,y,q},f_{1}^{x,y,q},f_{2}^{x,y,q}\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\right|\gg\delta\quad\text{for all }(x,y)\in\mathcal{P}.

By our second counting operator inverse theorem (Theorem 5.2), either M≪δ−O⁡(1)M\ll\delta^{-O(1)} or, for each pair (x,y)∈𝒫(x,y)\in\mathcal{P}, there exists αx,y∈𝕋\alpha_{x,y}\in\mathbb{T} and qx,y≪δ−O⁡(1)q_{x,y}\ll\delta^{-O(1)} with ‖qx,y​αx,y‖𝕋≪δ−O⁡(1)/M2\mathopen{}\left\|q_{x,y}\alpha_{x,y}\mathclose{}\right\|_{\mathbb{T}}\ll\delta^{-O(1)}/M^{2} and such that

𝔼x′∈[M]|𝔼y′∈[2​M2]f2x,y,q(x′,y′)e(αx,yy′)|≫δO⁡(1).\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\in[M]}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{y^{\prime}\in[2M^{2}]}f^{x,y,q}_{2}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})e\mathopen{}\left(\alpha_{x,y}y^{\prime}\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\right|\gg\delta^{O(1)}.

Notice that we can ignore the possibility that M≪δ−O⁡(1)M\ll\delta^{-O(1)}, since in this case all positive integers M~\widetilde{M} satisfy M~≫δO⁡(1)​M\widetilde{M}\gg\delta^{O(1)}M. Pigeon-holing in the major arcs, as in Lemma 4.3, we obtain α∈𝕋\alpha\in\mathbb{T} and q~≪δ−O⁡(1)\tilde{q}\ll\delta^{-O(1)} with ‖q~​α‖𝕋≪δ−O⁡(1)/M2\mathopen{}\left\|\tilde{q}\alpha\mathclose{}\right\|_{\mathbb{T}}\ll\delta^{-O(1)}/M^{2} and such that

(5.4) ∑x,y𝔼x′∈[M]|𝔼y′∈[2​M2]f2x,y,q(x′,y′)e(αy′)|≫δO⁡(1)N1N2.\sum_{x,y}\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\in[M]}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{y^{\prime}\in[2M^{2}]}f^{x,y,q}_{2}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})e\mathopen{}\left(\alpha y^{\prime}\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\right|\gg\delta^{O(1)}N_{1}N_{2}.

|e(αy′)−e(α(y′+q~2d~))|≪δ−O⁡(1)|d~|/M2.\mathopen{}\left|e\mathopen{}\left(\alpha y^{\prime}\mathclose{}\right)-e\mathopen{}\left(\alpha(y^{\prime}+\tilde{q}^{2}\tilde{d})\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\right|\ll\delta^{-O(1)}|\tilde{d}|/M^{2}.

Combining this with the fact that the set of pairs (x,y)(x,y) that contribute to (5.4) is contained in [−2​N1,2​N1]×[−2​N2,2​N2][-2N_{1},2N_{1}]\times[-2N_{2},2N_{2}], we deduce that for any positive integer M~\widetilde{M}, we either have M~≫δO⁡(1)​M\widetilde{M}\gg\delta^{O(1)}M or

𝔼y′∈[2​M2]fx,y,q2(x′,y′)𝔼d~∈[M~2]e(α(y′+q~2d~))=𝔼d~∈[M~2]𝔼y′−q~2​d~∈[2​M2]fx,y,q2(x′,y′−q~2d~)e(αy′).\mathbb{E}_{y^{\prime}\in[2M^{2}]}f^{x,y,q}_{2}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{d}\in[\widetilde{M}^{2}]}e\mathopen{}\left(\alpha(y^{\prime}+\tilde{q}^{2}\tilde{d})\mathclose{}\right)\\ =\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{d}\in[\widetilde{M}^{2}]}\mathbb{E}_{y^{\prime}-\tilde{q}^{2}\tilde{d}\in[2M^{2}]}f^{x,y,q}_{2}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}-\tilde{q}^{2}\tilde{d})e\mathopen{}\left(\alpha y^{\prime}\mathclose{}\right).

Hence, estimating the symmetric difference of the sets of summands gives that

𝔼y′∈[2​M2]fx,y,q2(x′,y′)𝔼d~∈[M~2]e(α(y′+q~2d~))=𝔼y′∈[2​M2]𝔼d~∈[M~2]fx,y,q2(x′,y′−q~2d~)e(αy′)+O(q~2​M~2M2).\mathbb{E}_{y^{\prime}\in[2M^{2}]}f^{x,y,q}_{2}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{d}\in[\widetilde{M}^{2}]}e\mathopen{}\left(\alpha(y^{\prime}+\tilde{q}^{2}\tilde{d})\mathclose{}\right)\\ =\mathbb{E}_{y^{\prime}\in[2M^{2}]}\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{d}\in[\widetilde{M}^{2}]}f^{x,y,q}_{2}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}-\tilde{q}^{2}\tilde{d})e\mathopen{}\left(\alpha y^{\prime}\mathclose{}\right)+O\mathopen{}\left(\frac{\tilde{q}^{2}\widetilde{M}^{2}}{M^{2}}\mathclose{}\right).

It follows that either M~≫δO⁡(1)​M\widetilde{M}\gg\delta^{O(1)}M or we have

∑x,y𝔼x′∈[M]|𝔼y′∈[2​M2]𝔼d~∈[M~2]f2x,y,q(x′,y′−q~2d~)e(αy′)|≫δO⁡(1)N1N2.\sum_{x,y}\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\in[M]}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{y^{\prime}\in[2M^{2}]}\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{d}\in[\widetilde{M}^{2}]}f^{x,y,q}_{2}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}-\tilde{q}^{2}\tilde{d})e\mathopen{}\left(\alpha y^{\prime}\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\right|\gg\delta^{O(1)}N_{1}N_{2}.

𝔼x′∈[M]𝔼y′∈[2​M2]∑x,y|𝔼d~∈[M~2]f2x,y,q(x′,y′−q~2d~)|≫δO⁡(1)N1N2.\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\in[M]}\mathbb{E}_{y^{\prime}\in[2M^{2}]}\sum_{x,y}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{d}\in[\widetilde{M}^{2}]}f^{x,y,q}_{2}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}-\tilde{q}^{2}\tilde{d})\mathclose{}\right|\gg\delta^{O(1)}N_{1}N_{2}.

Taking a maximum over x′x^{\prime} and y′y^{\prime}, then expanding the definition of each f2x,y,qf_{2}^{x,y,q} and changing variables, we have

∑x,y|𝔼d~∈[M~2]f2(x,y−q2q~2d~)|≫δO⁡(1)N1N2.\sum_{x,y}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{d}\in[\widetilde{M}^{2}]}f_{2}(x,y-q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2}\tilde{d})\mathclose{}\right|\gg\delta^{O(1)}N_{1}N_{2}.

An application of Cauchy–Schwarz to double the d~\tilde{d} variables then yields

δO⁡(1)​N1​N2≪∑x,y𝔼d~1,d~2∈[M~2]​f2​(x,y−q2​q~2​d~1)​f2​(x,y−q2​q~2​d~2)¯⩽∑x,y|𝔼d~1,d~2∈[M~2]f2(x,y+q2q~2(d~1−d~2))|\delta^{O(1)}N_{1}N_{2}\ll\sum_{x,y}\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{d}_{1},\tilde{d}_{2}\in[\widetilde{M}^{2}]}f_{2}(x,y-q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2}\tilde{d}_{1})\overline{f_{2}(x,y-q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2}\tilde{d}_{2})}\\ \leqslant\sum_{x,y}\mathopen{}\left|\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{d}_{1},\tilde{d}_{2}\in[\widetilde{M}^{2}]}f_{2}\mathopen{}\left(x,y+q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2}(\tilde{d}_{1}-\tilde{d}_{2})\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\right|

This gives (5.2), on recalling the definition (A.7) of the Fejér kernel μH\mu_{H}. ∎

We end this section by deriving the inverse theorem claimed in our introduction (Theorem 1.4), where there is no occurrence of the Fejér kernel μN\mu_{N} in the counting operator.

Proof of Theorem 1.4.

Set M:=⌈2​δ−1​N⌉M:=\mathopen{}\left\lceil 2\delta^{-1}N\mathclose{}\right\rceil. Due to the support of the fif_{i}, if

f0​(x,y)​f1​(x+d,y)​f2​(x,y+d2)≠0f_{0}(x,y)f_{1}(x+d,y)f_{2}(x,y+d^{2})\neq 0

then x∈[N]x\in[N], y∈[N2]y\in[N^{2}] and |d|<N|d|<N. It follows that

|f0(x,y)f1(x+d,y)f2(x,y+d2)−f0(x,y)f1(x+d,y)f2(x,y+d2)MμM(d)|⩽δ2​1[N]​(x)​1[N2]​(y).\mathopen{}\left|f_{0}(x,y)f_{1}(x+d,y)f_{2}(x,y+d^{2})-f_{0}(x,y)f_{1}(x+d,y)f_{2}(x,y+d^{2})M\mu_{M}(d)\mathclose{}\right|\\ \leqslant\tfrac{\delta}{2}1_{[N]}(x)1_{[N^{2}]}(y).

Thus the hypothesis (1.2) implies that

|ΛM(f0,f1,f2)|≫δN4M4≫δO⁡(1).\mathopen{}\left|\Lambda_{M}(f_{0},f_{1},f_{2})\mathclose{}\right|\gg\delta\tfrac{N^{4}}{M^{4}}\gg\delta^{O(1)}.

Applying Theorem 5.1 and Theorem 5.2, either N≪δ−O⁡(1)N\ll\delta^{-O(1)} or there exist α,β∈𝕋\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{T} and q1,q2≪δ−O⁡(1)q_{1},q_{2}\ll\delta^{-O(1)} such that ‖q1​α‖≪δ−O⁡(1)/N\mathopen{}\left\|q_{1}\alpha\mathclose{}\right\|\ll\delta^{-O(1)}/N and ‖q2​β‖≪δ−O⁡(1)/N2\mathopen{}\left\|q_{2}\beta\mathclose{}\right\|\ll\delta^{-O(1)}/N^{2}, as well as (1.3) holds. The theorem follows on taking q:=q1​q2q:=q_{1}q_{2}. ∎

6. Energy increment

We are now in a position to run an energy increment argument in order to obtain a modified counting operator that is close to our original count: see our outline in §2 for more on this. Green and Tao [GT12] call the argument underlying the following result a local Koopman-von Neuman theorem.

Theorem 6.1 (Energy increment to a subprogression).

Let 0<ε⩽1/20<\varepsilon\leqslant 1/2 and let f0,f1,f2:ℤ2→ℂf_{0},f_{1},f_{2}:\mathbb{Z}^{2}\to\mathbb{C} be 1-bounded functions, each with support contained in [N1]×[N2][N_{1}]\times[N_{2}] where N1⩾N21/2N_{1}\geqslant N_{2}^{1/2}. Then either N2⩽exp(ε−O⁡(1))N_{2}\leqslant\exp\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{-O(1)}\mathclose{}\right), or there exist q⩽exp(ε−O⁡(1))q\leqslant\exp\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{-O(1)}\mathclose{}\right) and M⩾N21/2/exp(ε−O⁡(1))M\geqslant N_{2}^{1/2}/\exp\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{-O(1)}\mathclose{}\right) such that

(6.1) |∑x,y,dμε​M(d)f0(x,y)f1(x+qd,y)[f2(x,y+q2d2)−∑d~μM2(d~)f2(x,y+q2(d~+d2))]|⩽ε​N1​N2.\biggl|\sum_{x,y,d}\mu_{\varepsilon M}(d)f_{0}(x,y)f_{1}(x+qd,y)\Bigl[f_{2}\mathopen{}\left(x,y+q^{2}d^{2}\mathclose{}\right)-\sum_{\tilde{d}}\mu_{M^{2}}(\tilde{d})f_{2}\mathopen{}\left(x,y+q^{2}\mathopen{}\left(\tilde{d}+d^{2}\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\right)\Bigr]\biggr|\\ \leqslant\varepsilon N_{1}N_{2}.

Moreover, we may choose MM sufficiently small to ensure that q​M⩽ε​N21/2qM\leqslant\varepsilon N_{2}^{1/2}. Here με​M\mu_{\varepsilon M} and μM2\mu_{M^{2}} denote Fejér kernels, as defined in (A.7).

Proof.

We perform an iterative procedure. At stage 0, we take q=q0:=1q=q_{0}:=1 and M=M0:=⌊ε​N21/2⌋M=M_{0}:=\lfloor\varepsilon N_{2}^{1/2}\rfloor. Suppose that at stage nn of our iteration we have a positive integers q=qn⩽ε−O⁡(n)q=q_{n}\leqslant\varepsilon^{-O(n)} and M=Mn∈[εO⁡(n+1)​N21/2,ε​N21/2/q]M=M_{n}\in[\varepsilon^{O(n+1)}N_{2}^{1/2},\varepsilon N_{2}^{1/2}/q] that satisfy the energy lower bound

(6.2) ∑x,y|∑d~f2​(x,y+q2​d~)​μM2​(d~)|2≫n​εO⁡(1)​N1​N2.\sum_{x,y}\biggl|\sum_{\tilde{d}}f_{2}(x,y+q^{2}\tilde{d})\mu_{M^{2}}(\tilde{d})\biggr|^{2}\gg n\varepsilon^{O(1)}N_{1}N_{2}.

Given this, we query whether (6.1) holds or not. If (6.1) holds, then the process terminates. Therefore suppose that (6.1) does not hold.

Write

g2(x,y):=f2(x,y)−∑d~μM2(d~)f2(x,y+q2d~),g_{2}(x,y):=f_{2}\mathopen{}\left(x,y\mathclose{}\right)-\sum_{\tilde{d}}\mu_{M^{2}}(\tilde{d})f_{2}\mathopen{}\left(x,y+q^{2}\tilde{d}\mathclose{}\right),

which is a function with support contained in [−N1,N1]×[−N2,N2][-N_{1},N_{1}]\times[-N_{2},N_{2}], since q2​M2⩽N2q^{2}M^{2}\leqslant N_{2}. Applying the inverse theorem for our asymmetric counting operator (Theorem 5.3), there exists a positive integer q~\tilde{q} with q~⩽ε−O⁡(1)\tilde{q}\leqslant\varepsilon^{-O(1)} such that for any positive integer M~\widetilde{M}, either M~⩾εO⁡(1)​M\widetilde{M}\geqslant\varepsilon^{O(1)}M or

(6.3) ∑x,y|∑d~μM~2(d~)g2(x,y+q2q~2d~)|≫εO⁡(1)N1N2.\sum_{x,y}\mathopen{}\left|\sum_{\tilde{d}}\mu_{\widetilde{M}^{2}}(\tilde{d})g_{2}(x,y+q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2}\tilde{d})\mathclose{}\right|\gg\varepsilon^{O(1)}N_{1}N_{2}.

Provided that it is not the case that M≪ε−O⁡(1)M\ll\varepsilon^{-O(1)}, we can find a positive integer M~⩾εO⁡(1)​M\widetilde{M}\geqslant\varepsilon^{O(1)}M sufficiently small to guarantee (6.3). If M≪ε−O⁡(1)M\ll\varepsilon^{-O(1)} then the process terminates.

On writing f2x​(y):=f2​(x,y)f_{2}^{x}(y):=f_{2}(x,y) and μq,H​(y):=1q⋅ℤ​(y)​μH​(y/q)\mu_{q,H}(y):=1_{q\cdot\mathbb{Z}}(y)\mu_{H}(y/q), we may expand the definition of g2g_{2} to re-formulate (6.3) as88 8 Here we have normalised the L1​(ℤ)L^{1}(\mathbb{Z}) norm as in (A.1).

∑x‖f2x∗μq2​q~2,M~2−f2x∗μq2,M2∗μq2​q~2,M~2‖1≫εO⁡(1)​N1​N2.\sum_{x}\mathopen{}\left\|f_{2}^{x}*\mu_{q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2},\widetilde{M}^{2}}-f_{2}^{x}*\mu_{q^{2},M^{2}}*\mu_{q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2},\widetilde{M}^{2}}\mathclose{}\right\|_{1}\gg\varepsilon^{O(1)}N_{1}N_{2}.

One can check that we have the bound

‖μq2,M2∗μq2​q~2,M~2−μq2,M2‖1≪q~2​M~2M2+q~4​M~4M4.\mathopen{}\left\|\mu_{q^{2},M^{2}}*\mu_{q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2},\widetilde{M}^{2}}-\mu_{q^{2},M^{2}}\mathclose{}\right\|_{1}\ll\frac{\tilde{q}^{2}\widetilde{M}^{2}}{M^{2}}+\frac{\tilde{q}^{4}\widetilde{M}^{4}}{M^{4}}.

Decreasing M~\widetilde{M} if necessary, but still retaining a lower bound of the form M~⩾εO⁡(1)​M\widetilde{M}\geqslant\varepsilon^{O(1)}M, we have

∑x‖f2x∗μq2​q~2,M~2−f2x∗μq2,M2‖1≫εO⁡(1)​N1​N2.\sum_{x}\mathopen{}\left\|f_{2}^{x}*\mu_{q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2},\widetilde{M}^{2}}-f_{2}^{x}*\mu_{q^{2},M^{2}}\mathclose{}\right\|_{1}\gg\varepsilon^{O(1)}N_{1}N_{2}.

Applying the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality then gives

∑x‖f2x∗μq2​q~2,M~2−f2x∗μq2,M2‖22≫εO⁡(1)​N1​N2.\sum_{x}\mathopen{}\left\|f_{2}^{x}*\mu_{q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2},\widetilde{M}^{2}}-f_{2}^{x}*\mu_{q^{2},M^{2}}\mathclose{}\right\|_{2}^{2}\gg\varepsilon^{O(1)}N_{1}N_{2}.

We wish to replace the above, which measures the energy of a difference of two functions f−gf-g, with the difference of their energies ‖f‖22−‖g‖22\mathopen{}\left\|f\mathclose{}\right\|_{2}^{2}-\mathopen{}\left\|g\mathclose{}\right\|_{2}^{2}. From Pythagoreans’ theorem, we know that to make this substitution we must show that f−gf-g and gg are (approximately) orthogonal. More concretely, writing L2L^{2}-norms in terms of inner products, we have

(6.4) ‖f2x∗μq2​q~2,M~2‖22−‖f2x∗μq2,M2‖22=‖f2x∗μq2​q~2,M~2−f2x∗μq2,M2‖22−2​Re⁡⟨f2x∗μq2,M2,f2x∗(μq2,M2−μq2​q~2,M~2)⟩.\big\|f_{2}^{x}*\mu_{q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2},\widetilde{M}^{2}}\big\|_{2}^{2}-\big\|f_{2}^{x}*\mu_{q^{2},M^{2}}\big\|_{2}^{2}=\big\|f_{2}^{x}*\mu_{q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2},\widetilde{M}^{2}}-f_{2}^{x}*\mu_{q^{2},M^{2}}\big\|_{2}^{2}\\ -2\operatorname{Re}\bigl\langle f_{2}^{x}*\mu_{q^{2},M^{2}},f_{2}^{x}*\bigl(\mu_{q^{2},M^{2}}-\mu_{q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2},\widetilde{M}^{2}}\bigr)\bigr\rangle.

So we wish to show that the latter inner product is small.

Suppose otherwise, so that the inner product in (6.4) is at least δ​‖f2x‖22\delta\mathopen{}\left\|f_{2}^{x}\mathclose{}\right\|_{2}^{2}. Then Parseval’s identity and the convolution identity give

δ​‖f2x‖22⩽Re⁡⟨f2x∗μq2,M2,f2x∗(μq2,M2−μq2​q~2,M~2)⟩=∫𝕋|f^x2(α)|2μ^q2,M2(α)[μ^q2,M2(α)−μ^q2​q~2,M~2(α)]dα⩽‖f2x‖22supα(μ^q2,M2(α)[μ^q2,M2(α)−μ^q2​q~2,M~2(α)]).\delta\mathopen{}\left\|f_{2}^{x}\mathclose{}\right\|_{2}^{2}\leqslant\operatorname{Re}\bigl\langle f_{2}^{x}*\mu_{q^{2},M^{2}},f_{2}^{x}*\bigl(\mu_{q^{2},M^{2}}-\mu_{q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2},\widetilde{M}^{2}}\bigr)\bigr\rangle\\ =\int_{\mathbb{T}}\bigl|\widehat{f}^{x}_{2}(\alpha)\bigr|^{2}\widehat{\mu}_{q^{2},M^{2}}(\alpha)\mathopen{}\left[\widehat{\mu}_{q^{2},M^{2}}(\alpha)-\widehat{\mu}_{q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2},\widetilde{M}^{2}}(\alpha)\mathclose{}\right]\mathrm{d}\alpha\\ \leqslant\mathopen{}\left\|f_{2}^{x}\mathclose{}\right\|_{2}^{2}\sup_{\alpha}\mathopen{}\left(\widehat{\mu}_{q^{2},M^{2}}(\alpha)\mathopen{}\left[\widehat{\mu}_{q^{2},M^{2}}(\alpha)-\widehat{\mu}_{q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2},\widetilde{M}^{2}}(\alpha)\mathclose{}\right]\mathclose{}\right).

By non-negativity of μ^q2,M2\widehat{\mu}_{q^{2},M^{2}}, there exists α∈𝕋\alpha\in\mathbb{T} such that both of the following hold

μ^q2,M2​(α)⩾δandμ^q2,M2​(α)−μ^q2​q~2,M~2​(α)⩾δ.\widehat{\mu}_{q^{2},M^{2}}(\alpha)\geqslant\delta\quad\text{and}\quad\widehat{\mu}_{q^{2},M^{2}}(\alpha)-\widehat{\mu}_{q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2},\widetilde{M}^{2}}(\alpha)\geqslant\delta.

Yet, we know from summing the geometric series that if

M−4|1^[M2](q2α)|2=μ^q2,M2(α)⩾δ,M^{-4}\mathopen{}\left|\hat{1}_{[M^{2}]}(q^{2}\alpha)\mathclose{}\right|^{2}=\widehat{\mu}_{q^{2},M^{2}}(\alpha)\geqslant\delta,

then ‖q2α‖𝕋⩽δ−1/2/M2\mathopen{}\left\|q^{2}\alpha\mathclose{}\right\|_{\mathbb{T}}\leqslant\delta^{-1/2}/M^{2}. Yet, for such values of α\alpha, we have

μ^q2​q~2,M~2​(α)=|𝔼d~∈[M~2]​e​(α​q2​q~2​d~)|2⩾(1−2​π​q~2​M~2δ1/2​M2)2⩾1−4​π​q~2​M~2δ1/2​M2.\widehat{\mu}_{q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2},\widetilde{M}^{2}}(\alpha)=\bigl|\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{d}\in[\widetilde{M}^{2}]}e(\alpha q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2}\tilde{d})\bigr|^{2}\geqslant\bigl(1-\frac{2\pi\tilde{q}^{2}\widetilde{M}^{2}}{\delta^{1/2}M^{2}}\bigr)^{2}\geqslant 1-\frac{4\pi\tilde{q}^{2}\widetilde{M}^{2}}{\delta^{1/2}M^{2}}.

Thus, taking δ=(5​π​q~2​M~2/M2)2/3\delta=(5\pi\tilde{q}^{2}\widetilde{M}^{2}/M^{2})^{2/3} gives the contradiction that such values of α\alpha satisfy μ^q2​q~2,M~2​(α)>1−δ\widehat{\mu}_{q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2},\widetilde{M}^{2}}(\alpha)>1-\delta and μ^q2,M2​(α)>1\widehat{\mu}_{q^{2},M^{2}}(\alpha)>1.

We have therefore deduced that

Re⟨f2x∗μq2,M2,f2x∗(μq2,M2−μq2​q~2,M~2)⟩≪(q~​M~M)4/3‖f2x‖22.\operatorname{Re}\mathopen{}\left\langle f_{2}^{x}*\mu_{q^{2},M^{2}},f_{2}^{x}*\mathopen{}\left(\mu_{q^{2},M^{2}}-\mu_{q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2},\widetilde{M}^{2}}\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\right\rangle\ll\mathopen{}\left(\tfrac{\tilde{q}\widetilde{M}}{M}\mathclose{}\right)^{4/3}\mathopen{}\left\|f_{2}^{x}\mathclose{}\right\|_{2}^{2}.

Putting all of the above together, we have that

∑x(∥f2x∗μq2​q~2,M~2∥22−‖f2x∗μq2,M2‖22)⩾Ω(εO⁡(1)N1N2)−O((q~​M~M)4/3N1N2).\sum_{x}\mathopen{}\left(\big\|f_{2}^{x}*\mu_{q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2},\widetilde{M}^{2}}\big\|_{2}^{2}-\mathopen{}\left\|f_{2}^{x}*\mu_{q^{2},M^{2}}\mathclose{}\right\|_{2}^{2}\mathclose{}\right)\geqslant\Omega\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{O(1)}N_{1}N_{2}\mathclose{}\right)-O\mathopen{}\left(\mathopen{}\left(\tfrac{\tilde{q}\widetilde{M}}{M}\mathclose{}\right)^{4/3}N_{1}N_{2}\mathclose{}\right).

Decreasing M~\widetilde{M} if necessary, but still retaining a lower bound of the form M~⩾εO⁡(1)​M\widetilde{M}\geqslant\varepsilon^{O(1)}M, we obtain the energy increment

∑x∥f2x∗μq2​q~2,M~2∥22⩾∑x∥f2x∗μq2,M2∥22+Ω(εO⁡(1)N1N2).\sum_{x}\big\|f_{2}^{x}*\mu_{q^{2}\tilde{q}^{2},\widetilde{M}^{2}}\big\|_{2}^{2}\geqslant\sum_{x}\big\|f_{2}^{x}*\mu_{q^{2},M^{2}}\big\|_{2}^{2}+\Omega\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{O(1)}N_{1}N_{2}\mathclose{}\right).

With this bound in hand, our inductive hypotheses are satisfied (see (6.2)), and our procedure iterates to the next stage.

Since the energy (6.2) is bounded above by N1​N2N_{1}N_{2}, our procedure must terminate at some stage n≪εO⁡(1)n\ll\varepsilon^{O(1)}, yielding either M=Mn≪ε−O⁡(1)M=M_{n}\ll\varepsilon^{-O(1)} or (6.1). Unpacking the rate at which q=qnq=q_{n} and M=MnM=M_{n} change, the former possibility leads to N⩽exp⁡(ε−O⁡(1))N\leqslant\exp(\varepsilon^{-O(1)}), whilst the latter gives our other desired outcome. ∎

7. Obtaining a popular difference

Finally we prove the remaining results claimed in our introduction §1.

Theorem 7.1 (Existence of a popular difference).

Let A⊂[N1]×[N2]A\subset[N_{1}]\times[N_{2}] with |A|⩾δ​N1​N2|A|\geqslant\delta N_{1}N_{2} and N1⩾N21/2N_{1}\geqslant N_{2}^{1/2}. Given 0<ε⩽1/20<\varepsilon\leqslant 1/2, either N2⩽exp(ε−O⁡(1))N_{2}\leqslant\exp\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{-O(1)}\mathclose{}\right) or there exist q⩽exp(ε−O⁡(1))q\leqslant\exp\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{-O(1)}\mathclose{}\right) and M⩾N21/2/exp(ε−O⁡(1))M\geqslant N_{2}^{1/2}/\exp\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{-O(1)}\mathclose{}\right) such that

∑x,y,dμM(d)1A(x,y)1A(x+qd,y)1A(x,y+q2d2)⩾(δ3−ε)N1N2.\sum_{x,y,d}\mu_{M}(d)1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x+qd,y)1_{A}(x,y+q^{2}d^{2})\geqslant\mathopen{}\left(\delta^{3}-\varepsilon\mathclose{}\right)N_{1}N_{2}.
Proof.

Let us apply our energy increment argument to 1A1_{A}, so we take f0=f1=f2=1Af_{0}=f_{1}=f_{2}=1_{A} in Theorem 6.1. This tells us that we either have N2⩽exp(ε−O⁡(1))N_{2}\leqslant\exp\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{-O(1)}\mathclose{}\right) or there exist q⩽exp(ε−O⁡(1))q\leqslant\exp\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{-O(1)}\mathclose{}\right) and M⩾N21/2/exp(ε−O⁡(1))M\geqslant N_{2}^{1/2}/\exp\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{-O(1)}\mathclose{}\right) such that q​M⩽ε​N21/2qM\leqslant\varepsilon N_{2}^{1/2} and

|∑x,y,dμε​M(d)1A(x,y)1A(x+qd,y)[1A(x,y+q2d2)−∑d~μM2(d~)1A(x,y+q2(d2+d~))]|⩽εN1N2.\biggl|\sum_{x,y,d}\mu_{\varepsilon M}(d)1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x+qd,y)\\ \biggl[1_{A}\mathopen{}\left(x,y+q^{2}d^{2}\mathclose{}\right)-\sum_{\tilde{d}}\mu_{M^{2}}(\tilde{d})1_{A}\mathopen{}\left(x,y+q^{2}\mathopen{}\left(d^{2}+\tilde{d}\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\right)\biggr]\biggr|\leqslant\varepsilon N_{1}N_{2}.

Focusing on the second counting operator, we have

∑x,y,dμε​M(d)1A(x,y)1A(x+qd,y)∑d~μM2(d~)1A(x,y+q2(d2+d~))=∑x,y,dμε​M(d)1A(x,y)1A(x+qd,y)∑d~μM2(d~−d2)1A(x,y+q2d~).\sum_{x,y,d}\mu_{\varepsilon M}(d)1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x+qd,y)\sum_{\tilde{d}}\mu_{M^{2}}\bigl(\tilde{d}\bigr)1_{A}\mathopen{}\left(x,y+q^{2}\mathopen{}\left(d^{2}+\tilde{d}\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\right)\\ =\sum_{x,y,d}\mu_{\varepsilon M}(d)1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x+qd,y)\sum_{\tilde{d}}\mu_{M^{2}}\mathopen{}\left(\tilde{d}-d^{2}\mathclose{}\right)1_{A}\mathopen{}\left(x,y+q^{2}\tilde{d}\mathclose{}\right).

The Lipschitz properties of μM2\mu_{M^{2}} give that

|μM2(d~−d2)−μM2(d~)|≪d2M−4.\mathopen{}\left|\mu_{M^{2}}\mathopen{}\left(\tilde{d}-d^{2}\mathclose{}\right)-\mu_{M^{2}}\bigl(\tilde{d}\bigr)\mathclose{}\right|\ll d^{2}M^{-4}.

Hence our restriction to |d|<ε​M|d|<\varepsilon M gives

∑x,y,dμε​M(d)1A(x,y)1A(x+qd,y)∑d~μM2(d~)1A(x,y+q2(d2+d~))⩾∑x,y,dμε​M(d)1A(x,y)1A(x+qd,y)∑d~μM2(d~)1A(x,y+q2d~)−O(εN1N2).\sum_{x,y,d}\mu_{\varepsilon M}(d)1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x+qd,y)\sum_{\tilde{d}}\mu_{M^{2}}\bigl(\tilde{d}\bigr)1_{A}\mathopen{}\left(x,y+q^{2}\mathopen{}\left(d^{2}+\tilde{d}\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\right)\\ \geqslant\sum_{x,y,d}\mu_{\varepsilon M}(d)1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x+qd,y)\sum_{\tilde{d}}\mu_{M^{2}}\bigl(\tilde{d}\bigr)1_{A}\mathopen{}\left(x,y+q^{2}\tilde{d}\mathclose{}\right)-O\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon N_{1}N_{2}\mathclose{}\right).

Expanding the definition (A.7) of the Fejér kernel, then changing variables, we have

∑x,y,dμε​M(d)1A(x,y)1A(x+qd,y)∑d~μM2(d~)1A(x,y+q2d~)⩾∑x,y𝔼d1,d2∈[ε​M]​𝔼d~1,d~2∈[M2]​1A​(x+q​d1,y+q2​d~1)1A​(x+q​d2,y+q2​d~1)​1A​(x+q​d1,y+q2​d~2).\sum_{x,y,d}\mu_{\varepsilon M}(d)1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x+qd,y)\sum_{\tilde{d}}\mu_{M^{2}}\bigl(\tilde{d}\bigr)1_{A}\mathopen{}\left(x,y+q^{2}\tilde{d}\mathclose{}\right)\\ \geqslant\sum_{x,y}\mathbb{E}_{d_{1},d_{2}\in[\varepsilon M]}\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{d}_{1},\tilde{d}_{2}\in[M^{2}]}1_{A}\bigl(x+qd_{1},y+q^{2}\tilde{d}_{1}\bigr)\\ 1_{A}\bigl(x+qd_{2},y+q^{2}\tilde{d}_{1}\bigr)1_{A}\bigl(x+qd_{1},y+q^{2}\tilde{d}_{2}\bigr).

By an application of Hölder’s inequality, sometimes termed the Blakley-Roy inequality99 9 See this discussion https://mathoverflow.net/questions/189222., we have

𝔼d1,d2∈[ε​M]​𝔼d~1,d~2∈[M2]​1A​(x+q​d1,y+q2​d~1)​1A​(x+q​d2,y+q2​d~1)​1A​(x+q​d1,y+q2​d~2)⩾(𝔼d∈[ε​M]𝔼d~∈[M2]1A(x+qd,y+q2d~))3.\mathbb{E}_{d_{1},d_{2}\in[\varepsilon M]}\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{d}_{1},\tilde{d}_{2}\in[M^{2}]}1_{A}(x+qd_{1},y+q^{2}\tilde{d}_{1})1_{A}(x+qd_{2},y+q^{2}\tilde{d}_{1})1_{A}(x+qd_{1},y+q^{2}\tilde{d}_{2})\\ \geqslant\mathopen{}\left(\mathbb{E}_{d\in[\varepsilon M]}\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{d}\in[M^{2}]}1_{A}(x+qd,y+q^{2}\tilde{d})\mathclose{}\right)^{3}.

If the sum inside the cube is non-zero, then (because A⊂[N1]×[N2]A\subset[N_{1}]\times[N_{2}]) we have

(x,y)∈(−q​ε​M,N1)×(−q2​M2,N2)⊂(−ε​N1,N1)×(−ε​N2,N2).(x,y)\in(-q\varepsilon M,N_{1})\times(-q^{2}M^{2},N_{2})\subset(-\varepsilon N_{1},N_{1})\times(-\varepsilon N_{2},N_{2}).

So, again by Hölder’s inequality,

∑x,y(𝔼d∈[ε​M]𝔼d~∈[M2]1A(x+qd,y+q2d~))3⩾N1−2N2−2(1+ε)−4(∑x,y𝔼d∈[M]𝔼d~∈[M2]1A(x+qd,y+q2d~))3⩾δ3​N1​N2​(1−ε)4.\sum_{x,y}\mathopen{}\left(\mathbb{E}_{d\in[\varepsilon M]}\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{d}\in[M^{2}]}1_{A}(x+qd,y+q^{2}\tilde{d})\mathclose{}\right)^{3}\\ \geqslant N_{1}^{-2}N_{2}^{-2}(1+\varepsilon)^{-4}\mathopen{}\left(\sum_{x,y}\mathbb{E}_{d\in[M]}\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{d}\in[M^{2}]}1_{A}(x+qd,y+q^{2}\tilde{d})\mathclose{}\right)^{3}\\ \geqslant\delta^{3}N_{1}N_{2}(1-\varepsilon)^{4}.

Putting everything together gives

∑x,y,dμε​M(d)1A(x,y)1A(x+qd,y)1A(x,y+q2d2)⩾(δ3−O(ε))N1N2,\sum_{x,y,d}\mu_{\varepsilon M}(d)1_{A}(x,y)1_{A}(x+qd,y)1_{A}(x,y+q^{2}d^{2})\geqslant\mathopen{}\left(\delta^{3}-O(\varepsilon)\mathclose{}\right)N_{1}N_{2},

as required. ∎

Taking N1=N2N_{1}=N_{2} in Theorem 7.1 yields Theorem 1.2. Taking N2=N12N_{2}=N_{1}^{2} yields the following, which is perhaps more natural.

Corollary 7.2.

Let A⊂[N]×[N2]A\subset[N]\times[N^{2}] with |A|⩾δ​N3|A|\geqslant\delta N^{3} and let 0<ε⩽1/20<\varepsilon\leqslant 1/2. Either N⩽exp(ε−O⁡(1))N\leqslant\exp\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{-O(1)}\mathclose{}\right) or there exists d≠0d\neq 0 such that

#{(x,y)∈A:(x+d,y),(x,y+d2)∈A}⩾(δ3−ε)N3.\#\mathopen{}\left\{(x,y)\in A:(x+d,y),(x,y+d^{2})\in A\mathclose{}\right\}\geqslant\mathopen{}\left(\delta^{3}-\varepsilon\mathclose{}\right)N^{3}.

From this we derive the existence of a one-dimensional popular common difference, which is claimed in Theorem 1.3.

Corollary 7.3 (Theorem 1.3, re-stated).

Let A⊂[N]A\subset[N] with |A|⩾δ​N|A|\geqslant\delta N and let 0<ε⩽1/20<\varepsilon\leqslant 1/2. Either N⩽exp(ε−O⁡(1))N\leqslant\exp\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{-O(1)}\mathclose{}\right) or there exists d≠0d\neq 0 such that

#{x∈A:x+d,x+d2∈A}⩾(δ3−ε)N.\#\mathopen{}\left\{x\in A:x+d,x+d^{2}\in A\mathclose{}\right\}\geqslant\mathopen{}\left(\delta^{3}-\varepsilon\mathclose{}\right)N.
Proof.

Define

A~:={(x,y)∈[N1/2]×[N]:x+y∈A}.\tilde{A}:=\mathopen{}\left\{(x,y)\in[N^{1/2}]\times[N]:x+y\in A\mathclose{}\right\}.

Let us bound the size of A~\tilde{A}. We have:

|A~|⩾∑a∈A∩(N1/2,N]∑x∈[N1/2]1[N](a−x)⩾(δN−N1/2)N1/2⩾(δ−ε)N3/2,|\tilde{A}|\geqslant\sum_{a\in A\cap(N^{1/2},N]}\sum_{x\in[N^{1/2}]}1_{[N]}(a-x)\geqslant\mathopen{}\left(\delta N-N^{1/2}\mathclose{}\right)N^{1/2}\geqslant(\delta-\varepsilon)N^{3/2},

or else N≪ε−O⁡(1)N\ll\varepsilon^{-O(1)}.

Applying Theorem 7.1, either N⩽exp(ε−O⁡(1))N\leqslant\exp\mathopen{}\left(\varepsilon^{-O(1)}\mathclose{}\right) or there exists an integer d≠0d\neq 0 such that

#{(x,y)∈[N1/2]×[N]:x+y,x+y+d,x+y+d2∈A}⩾((δ−ε)3−ε)N3/2.\#\mathopen{}\left\{(x,y)\in[N^{1/2}]\times[N]:x+y,\ x+y+d,\ x+y+d^{2}\in A\mathclose{}\right\}\geqslant\mathopen{}\left((\delta-\varepsilon)^{3}-\varepsilon\mathclose{}\right)N^{3/2}.

Taking a maximum over x∈[N1/2]x\in[N^{1/2}], we obtain some x0x_{0} such that

#{y∈[N]:x0+y,x0+y+d,x0+y+d2∈A}⩾((δ−ε)3−ε)N.\#\mathopen{}\left\{y\in[N]:x_{0}+y,\ x_{0}+y+d,\ x_{0}+y+d^{2}\in A\mathclose{}\right\}\geqslant\mathopen{}\left((\delta-\varepsilon)^{3}-\varepsilon\mathclose{}\right)N.

The result follows on observing that (by the binomial theorem) (δ−ε)3⩾δ3−4​ε(\delta-\varepsilon)^{3}\geqslant\delta^{3}-4\varepsilon. ∎

Appendix A Notation

A.1. Standard conventions

We use ℕ\mathbb{N} to denote the positive integers. For real X⩾1X\geqslant 1, write [X]={1,2,…,⌊X⌋}[X]=\{1,2,\ldots,\mathopen{}\left\lfloor X\right\rfloor\}. A complex-valued function is 1-bounded if the modulus of the function does not exceed 1.

We use counting measure on ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d}, so that for f,g:ℤd→ℂf,g:\mathbb{Z}^{d}\to\mathbb{C} we have

(A.1) ⟨f,g⟩:=∑xf(x)g⁡(x)¯and‖f‖Lp:=(∑x|f(x)|p)1p.\mathopen{}\left\langle f,g\mathclose{}\right\rangle:=\sum_{x}f(x)\overline{g(x)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathopen{}\left\|f\mathclose{}\right\|_{L^{p}}:=\biggl(\sum_{x}|f(x)|^{p}\biggr)^{\frac{1}{p}}.

Any sum of the form ∑x\sum_{x} is to be interpreted as a sum over ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d}. We use Haar probability measure on 𝕋d:=ℝd/ℤd\mathbb{T}^{d}:=\mathbb{R}^{d}/\mathbb{Z}^{d}, so that for measurable F:𝕋d→ℂF:\mathbb{T}^{d}\to\mathbb{C} we have

‖F‖Lp:=(∫𝕋d|F(α)|pdα)1p=(∫[0,1)d|F(α)|pdα)1p\mathopen{}\left\|F\mathclose{}\right\|_{L^{p}}:=\biggl(\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}|F(\alpha)|^{p}\mathrm{d}\alpha\biggr)^{\frac{1}{p}}=\biggl(\int_{[0,1)^{d}}|F(\alpha)|^{p}\mathrm{d}\alpha\biggr)^{\frac{1}{p}}

For α∈𝕋\alpha\in\mathbb{T} we write ‖α‖𝕋\mathopen{}\left\|\alpha\mathclose{}\right\|_{\mathbb{T}} for the distance to the nearest integer.

For a finite set SS and function f:S→ℂf:S\to\mathbb{C}, denote the average of ff over SS by

𝔼s∈S​f​(s):=1|S|​∑s∈Sf⁡(s).\mathbb{E}_{s\in S}f(s):=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{s\in S}f(s).

Given functions f,g:G→ℂf,g:G\to\mathbb{C} on an additive group with measure μG\mu_{G} we define their convolution by

(A.2) f∗g⁡(x):=∫Gf⁡(x−y)​g​(y)​d​μG,f*g(x):=\int_{G}f(x-y)g(y)\mathrm{d}\mu_{G},

when this makes sense. On the integers G=ℤG=\mathbb{Z}, we take μG\mu_{G} to be counting measure.

We define the Fourier transform of f:ℤd→ℂf:\mathbb{Z}^{d}\to\mathbb{C} by

(A.3) f^​(α):=∑xf⁡(x)​e​(α⋅x)(α∈𝕋d),\hat{f}(\alpha):=\sum_{x}f(x)e(\alpha\cdot x)\qquad(\alpha\in\mathbb{T}^{d}),

again, when this makes sense. Here e⁡(β)e(\beta) stands for e2​π​i​βe^{2\pi i\beta}.

The difference function of f:ℤd→ℂf:\mathbb{Z}^{d}\to\mathbb{C} with respect to h∈ℤdh\in\mathbb{Z}^{d} is the function Δh​f:ℤd→ℂ\Delta_{h}f:\mathbb{Z}^{d}\to\mathbb{C} given by

(A.4) Δh​f​(x)=f⁡(x)​f⁡(x+h)¯.\Delta_{h}f(x)=f(x)\overline{f(x+h)}.

Iterating, we set

Δh1,…,hs​f:=Δh1​…​Δhs​f.\Delta_{h_{1},\dots,h_{s}}f:=\Delta_{h_{1}}\dots\Delta_{h_{s}}f.

This allows us to define the Gowers UsU^{s}-norm

(A.5) ‖f‖Us​(ℤd):=(∑x,h1,…,hs∈ℤdΔh1,…,hsf(x))1/2s.\mathopen{}\left\|f\mathclose{}\right\|_{U^{s}(\mathbb{Z}^{d})}:=\mathopen{}\left(\sum_{x,h_{1},\dots,h_{s}\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}}\Delta_{h_{1},\dots,h_{s}}f(x)\mathclose{}\right)^{1/2^{s}}.

When S⊂ℤdS\subset\mathbb{Z}^{d} we define the localised Gowers UsU^{s}-norm

(A.6) ‖f‖Us​(S):=‖f​1S‖Us.\mathopen{}\left\|f\mathclose{}\right\|_{U^{s}(S)}:=\mathopen{}\left\|f1_{S}\mathclose{}\right\|_{U^{s}}.

For a function ff and positive-valued function gg, write f≪gf\ll g or f=O⁡(g)f=O(g) if there exists a constant CC such that |f⁡(x)|≤C​g​(x)|f(x)|\leq Cg(x) for all xx. We write f=Ω⁡(g)f=\Omega(g) if f≫gf\gg g. We sometimes opt for a more explicit approach, using CC to denote a large absolute constant, and cc to denote a small positive absolute constant. The values of CC and cc may change from line to line.

A.2. Local conventions

Up to normalisation, all of the above are well-used in the literature. Next we list notation specific to our paper. We have tried to minimise this in order to aid the casual reader.

For a real parameter H⩾1H\geqslant 1, we use μH:ℤ→[0,1]\mu_{H}:\mathbb{Z}\to[0,1] to represent the following normalised Fejér kernel

(A.7) μH(h):=1⌊H⌋(1−|h|⌊H⌋)+=(1[H]∗1−[H])​(h)⌊H⌋2.\mu_{H}(h):=\frac{1}{\mathopen{}\left\lfloor H\right\rfloor}\mathopen{}\left(1-\frac{|h|}{\mathopen{}\left\lfloor H\right\rfloor}\mathclose{}\right)_{+}=\frac{(1_{[H]}*1_{-[H]})(h)}{\mathopen{}\left\lfloor H\right\rfloor^{2}}.

Strictly speaking, “Fejér kernel” usually refers to the Fourier transform of this function, which is a function on the torus 𝕋\mathbb{T}. We adhere to our unconventional nomenclature since most of our arguments take place in ℤ\mathbb{Z}. For a multidimensional vector h∈ℤdh\in\mathbb{Z}^{d} we write

(A.8) μH​(h)=μH​(h1,…,hd):=μH​(h1)​⋯​μH​(hd).\mu_{H}(h)=\mu_{H}(h_{1},\dots,h_{d}):=\mu_{H}(h_{1})\dotsm\mu_{H}(h_{d}).

We observe that this is a probability measure on ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d} with support in the box (−H,H)d(-H,H)^{d}.

Define a counting operator on the functions f0,f1,f2:ℤ2→ℂf_{0},f_{1},f_{2}:\mathbb{Z}^{2}\to\mathbb{C} by

(A.9) ΛN​(f0,f1,f2):=𝔼x∈[N]​𝔼y∈[N2]​∑dμN​(d)​f0​(x,y)​f1​(x+d,y)​f2​(x,y+d2).\Lambda_{N}(f_{0},f_{1},f_{2}):=\mathbb{E}_{x\in[N]}\mathbb{E}_{y\in[N^{2}]}\sum_{d}\mu_{N}(d)f_{0}(x,y)f_{1}(x+d,y)f_{2}(x,y+d^{2}).

When the fif_{i} are all equal to ff we simply write ΛN​(f)\Lambda_{N}(f).
